flat-grant.label: A flat grant, paid to you
flat-grant.blurb: A set amount arrives each year and you buy your own supplies. Anything above the grant is yours to cover — and may be claimable as a medical expense at tax time.

cost-share.label: A percentage cost-share
cost-share.blurb: The program covers a share and you pay the rest, often up to an annual maximum. Low income usually reduces or removes your share.

supplies-in-kind.label: Supplies issued to you
supplies-in-kind.blurb: The program sends the supplies rather than reimbursing you, so you are registered rather than applying — and you do not buy them at retail.

categorical.label: Only if you qualify
categorical.blurb: There is no general program. Coverage runs through specific routes — seniors, social assistance, or a named condition — so the question is which category you fall into.

none.label: No ostomy-specific program
none.blurb: Nothing covers ostomy supplies directly here. Federal routes and tax credits may still help.

ON.name: Ontario
ON.amount: You receive $975 per ostomy per year, paid in two instalments. That rises to $1,300 if you live in a long-term care home or receive social assistance.
ON.howToApply: A physician or nurse practitioner examines you and confirms the ostomy, you both complete form 014-1945-67, and it goes to the Assistive Devices Program. The money is paid to you, not to a vendor, so you can buy supplies wherever you like.
ON.gatekeeper: A physician or nurse practitioner — an NSWOC signature is not required here, which differs from several other provinces.
ON.deadlines: Renew every two years; ADP sends paperwork about three months before expiry. Reviews take up to eight weeks, with the first payment within 30 days of approval.
ON.notes: A temporary ostomy only qualifies if it is needed for longer than six months. If you receive ODSP, the Mandatory Special Necessities benefit can cover costs above the grant — but only once the ADP grant is used up.

BC.name: British Columbia
BC.amount: After an income-based family deductible, PharmaCare pays 70% of eligible costs — 75% if a family member was born before 1940 — then 100% once you reach the family maximum.
BC.howToApply: There is no ostomy application. The step that matters is registering for Fair PharmaCare, which sets your deductible. Register at gov.bc.ca or on 1-800-663-7100, then coverage applies automatically at the till through an authorised provider.
BC.gatekeeper: Nobody clinical — registration and CRA income verification are the gate. The practical gatekeeper is a provider who can bill under a listed product code.
BC.deadlines: Return the mailed consent form within 30 days or registration does not complete. Deductibles run on the calendar year.
BC.notes: If you do not register for Fair PharmaCare you are assigned a $10,000 deductible by default, which means paying for everything yourself. Registering is the single highest-value thing a BC reader can do. Note that skin barriers, protectants, deodorants and cleansers are not covered — people routinely assume they are.

AB.name: Alberta
AB.amount: You pay 25% of the cost, up to a maximum of $500 per family per benefit year — after which AADL covers 100% for the rest of the year. The $500 is a ceiling on what you pay, not an amount you receive.
AB.howToApply: An AADL-approved authoriser assesses you and authorises the products; an approved vendor then bills AADL directly and charges you your share at the point of sale.
AB.gatekeeper: An AADL-approved authoriser — for ostomy products this is a registered nurse, and in practice usually an NSWOC.
AB.deadlines: The benefit year runs 1 July to 30 June.
AB.notes: Low-income Albertans and income-assistance recipients pay nothing at all. If you are excluded because another plan covers you fully — Veterans Affairs, NIHB, or WCB — that other plan is the route.

SK.name: Saskatchewan
SK.amount: The province pays 50% of eligible supplies within quantity limits, and you pay the other half. There is no annual dollar cap.
SK.howToApply: Referral from an ET/NSWOC nurse at a Saskatchewan stoma clinic. This is the only route in — a prescription from your family doctor will not register you, and there is no way to apply for yourself.
SK.gatekeeper: An ET/NSWOC nurse at a provincial stoma clinic. Registration comes before coverage.
SK.notes: Some people get supplies at no charge rather than at 50% — Paraplegia Program registrants, and holders of Supplementary Health Benefits through SAID, SIS or SEI. Worth asking about before assuming you pay half.

MB.name: Manitoba
MB.howToApply: You are registered by an NSWOC after surgery rather than applying yourself. The program then covers basic supplies in full and sends them to you — there is nothing to pay and nothing to claim back.
MB.gatekeeper: An NSWOC, who sets your supply list. Any change to that list also needs NSWOC approval.
MB.deadlines: Order at least two weeks ahead. You can request up to three months of supplies at a time.
MB.notes: There is no dollar figure here, and that is correct rather than missing — limits are set per product in quantities, not in money. Any number you find quoted for Manitoba is not a current benefit rate.

QC.name: Quebec
QC.amount: An annual lump sum of $1,510 for a permanent ostomy, or $1,007 for a temporary one. Paid per ostomy, so two stomas means two allocations.
QC.howToApply: You apply to RAMQ yourself. The only conditions are being insured under the Québec Health Insurance Plan and having had a colostomy, ileostomy or urostomy.
QC.gatekeeper: No clinical sign-off is needed to submit — you apply directly.
QC.deadlines: Amounts are indexed every 1 January. Temporary-ostomy payments are split — half when the application is accepted, then every six months until the stoma is closed.
QC.notes: If you hold a claim slip through social assistance you are reimbursed at actual cost instead of the lump sum. There is also a voluntary agreement that pays your supplier directly and ends the lump-sum payments — useful for some people, but it is a one-way switch worth understanding first.

NB.name: New Brunswick
NB.howToApply: There is no general ostomy program in New Brunswick. If you are a Social Development client with a qualifying health card, eligible supplies cost you nothing and the program pays pharmacies and suppliers directly. If you are not, this route is closed and the federal and tax options below are where to look.
NB.gatekeeper: Your Social Development health card is the gate — it must show the right supplementary or ostomy eligibility code.
NB.notes: Coverage is capped by monthly quantities per product rather than by dollars — for example a set number of wafers and pouches each month.

NS.name: Nova Scotia
NS.amount: Ostomy products are a listed Pharmacare benefit, so what you pay depends on which plan you are in rather than on an ostomy-specific rate.
NS.howToApply: Ostomy products are dispensed as prescriptions through a Nova Scotia pharmacy, so the route is a prescriber plus enrolment in a Pharmacare plan. Family Pharmacare is open to any resident without other drug coverage — worth knowing, because Nova Scotia is often described as having nothing for the general public, and that is not right.
NS.gatekeeper: A physician or nurse practitioner prescribes. An NSWOC is not a gatekeeper here. Plan enrolment is the real step.
NS.deadlines: Reimbursement claims must be submitted within six months of the prescription being dispensed — the most commonly missed deadline in the province.
NS.notes: If you are in active cancer treatment with a combined family income of $35,000 or less, the Boarding, Transportation and Ostomy program reimburses actual supply costs on top. Seniors and Income Assistance clients have their own cost-sharing rules.

PE.name: Prince Edward Island
PE.amount: Reimburses 60% to 100% of what you spend depending on household income, up to $2,400 per full program year.
PE.howToApply: A health care professional submits the Health Care Provider Registration Form for you. After that it is income-tested rather than clinical.
PE.gatekeeper: A health care professional — the program does not specifically require an NSWOC.
PE.deadlines: The program year runs 1 July to 30 June and you must re-apply before it expires or coverage stops. Old invoices are not accepted, so submit regularly rather than saving them up.
PE.notes: Joining part-way through the year pro-rates the maximum.

NL.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
NL.amount: Reimburses 75% of the retail cost of eligible items — but only for 65Plus Plan cardholders, meaning seniors receiving both Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
NL.howToApply: Enrolment happens automatically through your OAS and GIS status. You buy the supplies, keep the original prescription receipts, and claim the 75% back.
NL.gatekeeper: No separate assessor — a prescription and your 65Plus card are what is needed.
NL.notes: If you are under 65, or not receiving GIS, the official page does not name you as eligible for this subsidy. Check the other NLPDP plans and the federal routes below.

YT.name: Yukon
YT.howToApply: Your physician — or a community health nurse where there is no resident doctor — applies on your behalf, and pre-approval before you buy is expected. If you are 65 or over you are covered instead through Seniors Pharmacare, enrolled automatically.
YT.gatekeeper: A physician or community health nurse. Note that having an ostomy is not by itself a qualifying condition — coverage runs through a closed list of chronic diseases, and several common causes of ostomy are not on it. Confirm your specific diagnosis before assuming you are covered.
YT.deadlines: Apply before you buy. Purchases made outside Yukon without prior approval must be claimed within one year.
YT.notes: Yukon publishes no ostomy figure and no deductible amount on its own pages. Numbers circulate elsewhere; we are not repeating them, because we could not confirm them. Call the program to get your own numbers before planning around them.

NT.name: Northwest Territories
NT.amount: Seniors 60+ and lower-income bands pay nothing. Higher bands pay 25% of the cost up to a yearly family maximum of $500 to $1,500 depending on income band, after which the plan pays everything. There is no deductible on medical supplies.
NT.howToApply: Register under the Extended Health Benefits policy, which involves an income assessment — unless you are 60 or over, in which case you are enrolled on age. A prescriber then orders the supplies.
NT.gatekeeper: Program registration plus a prescription from a recognised health care prescriber.
NT.deadlines: Bands and maximums reset on 1 September.
NT.notes: Ostomy supplies are covered under general medical supplies rather than a named ostomy benefit. First Nations and Inuit residents go through NIHB instead.

NU.name: Nunavut
NU.howToApply: There is no ostomy-specific program. If you qualify under specified conditions or seniors coverage, prescribed medical supplies are covered including fitting and shipping — which matters a great deal in Nunavut. Most Nunavummiut are Inuit and are covered federally through NIHB instead.
NU.gatekeeper: A prescription is required either way.
NU.notes: Nunavut publishes no amount, cap, or per-item rate for supplies, and no list we could confirm of which conditions qualify. Call Extended Health Benefits on 867-645-8029 to ask whether your diagnosis is on the list rather than assuming either way.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for assessment by your NSWOC, surgeon, or physician. Fit, skin, and product choices depend on your body and your surgery — talk to your care team before changing anything. Funding amounts and eligibility rules change every year — always confirm on the official government page before planning around a number.

results.nihbBody: For registered First Nations and recognized Inuit, NIHB covers approved ostomy items subject to quantity limits and prior approval, and recognized providers bill NIHB directly so you do not pay upfront. This replaces the provincial route rather than topping it up. Ask about the exception process if you need more than the standard quantity — high output is a common reason.
results.deadlinesTitle: Dates that quietly cost people money
results.lastResortTitle: Your workplace plan gets billed first
results.lastResortBody: This territory is a payer of last resort, which means private or employer insurance has to be exhausted before the territorial program pays anything. Submit to your insurer first and keep the statement — you will need it.
results.dtcTitle: The Disability Tax Credit — worth applying for, but read the test first
results.dtcBody: Having an ostomy does not qualify you on its own, and a well-managed routine is often refused. The test is whether you are unable to manage bowel or bladder function, or it takes about three times longer than it would for someone of similar age without the impairment, at least 90% of the time, for a continuous 12 months — judged even with your appliances and routine in place. That means complications, leaks and time burden are what the form has to show. Only a medical doctor or nurse practitioner can certify it.
results.expensesTitle: Claim what you paid out of pocket — no approval needed
results.expensesBody: This one has no gate. Ostomy pads and supplies are listed eligible medical expenses, so whatever your province does not cover may be claimable on your return whether or not you have the Disability Tax Credit. Keep every receipt, including shipping where it is not covered.

1.q: How often should I empty or change my ostomy pouch?
1.a: Empty drainable pouches at around one-third to one-half full. Full system changes are often every few days, or sooner if you feel burning, itching, or a leak. Your NSWOC can help you find a wear time that suits your body — wear time varies a great deal between people and is not something to judge yourself against.

2.q: Can I customize an ostomy kit?
2.a: Yes. Start from a curated kit, adjust the quantities, add anything that was missing, and save your version — or subscribe so the restock keeps arriving on your own schedule.

3.q: How do ostomy supply subscriptions work?
3.a: On a product page, choose Subscribe & save, pick a frequency that matches your wear time, then check out like any order. Skip a delivery when you still have extras — no charge, nothing ships. Manage pause, skip, or cancel under Account → Subscriptions.

4.q: What belongs in an ostomy go-bag?
4.a: A spare barrier and pouch, soft wipes, disposal bags, and any skin protectant or adhesive remover you use — plus spare underwear or a liner if that helps you feel ready to be out.

5.q: What can I ask a pharmacist about my ostomy?
5.a: Everyday product and restock questions, in Ontario during business hours until 5 p.m. Eastern. Clinical concerns — fit, skin, and anything about the stoma itself — belong with your NSWOC or surgeon rather than a pharmacist.

fundingPage.modelsIntro: Almost every misunderstanding about ostomy funding comes from assuming your province works like a different one. There are really only four models.
fundingPage.toolIntro: Nothing you enter is saved or sent anywhere — this runs entirely in your browser.
fundingPage.federalHeading: Help that does not depend on where you live
fundingPage.dtcNote: The most valuable and most misunderstood item on this page — and the one people most often get refused.
fundingPage.dtcPoint1: Having an ostomy does not qualify you on its own. This is the part almost every summary gets wrong. A well-managed routine is frequently refused, and the CRA’s own guidance says so.
fundingPage.dtcPoint2: The test: you are unable to manage bowel or bladder function, or it takes you roughly three times longer than someone of similar age without the impairment, at least 90% of the time, for a continuous 12 months — assessed with your appliances and routine already in place.
fundingPage.dtcPoint3: So what gets approved is complications and time burden, not the stoma itself. Leaks, skin breakdown, repeated changes, night-time management, time lost from work — that is what belongs on the form.
fundingPage.dtcPoint4: Apply through the eliminating category — bowel or bladder function — not life-sustaining therapy. Only a medical doctor or nurse practitioner can certify it. Your NSWOC can help you describe your routine accurately, but cannot sign the form.
fundingPage.dtcPoint5: It is still worth applying: approval can be backdated up to ten years, and it unlocks the RDSP and the Canada Disability Benefit. A refusal costs you those too, which is why the wording matters so much.
fundingPage.dtcPoint6: If you are refused, the medical expense claim below needs no approval at all.
fundingPage.nihbPoint1: For registered First Nations and recognized Inuit, NIHB covers approved ostomy items subject to quantity limits and prior approval. Recognized providers bill NIHB directly, so there is no upfront cost to you.
fundingPage.nihbPoint2: This replaces the provincial route rather than topping it up — so start here rather than applying to your province first.
fundingPage.nihbPoint3: There is an exception process for quantities or items outside the standard list. High output is a common and legitimate reason to use it.
fundingPage.expensesHeading: Medical expenses on your tax return
fundingPage.expensesPoint1: Whatever your province does not cover may be claimable. Several provinces say so explicitly on their own program pages.
fundingPage.expensesPoint2: Keep receipts, including shipping where it is not covered.
fundingPage.ranOutHeading: The funding ran out before the year did
fundingPage.ranOut1Body: Often the fastest win is not more money but a better fit — fewer changes, longer wear time, less waste. An NSWOC can also tell you what actually gets approved in your region.
fundingPage.ranOut2Body: Hollister, Coloplast, and Convatec all run free support lines with samples and nurse access, regardless of where you buy. They will also help you navigate coverage.
fundingPage.ranOut3Heading: Check social assistance and disability routes
fundingPage.ranOut3Body: Provincial disability and social assistance programs sometimes top up ostomy coverage above the standard grant. This is worth asking about directly.
fundingPage.ranOut4Body: Ostomy Canada chapters know the local landscape, and some hold donated supplies. Treat second-hand product carefully — check the expiry date, that the inner packaging is unopened, that the size matches what you use, and ask how it was stored.
fundingPage.movingIntro: Nobody writes this down, and it catches people out. Moving resets your coverage entirely — different model, different amount, different forms, and often a different person who has to sign them.
fundingPage.before1: Claim anything outstanding — most programs will not pay across a move.
fundingPage.before2: Ask your NSWOC for a written summary of your current setup, sizes, and products. It shortens registration at the other end considerably.
fundingPage.before3: Stock up enough to cover the gap while new coverage is approved.
fundingPage.arrive1: Find an NSWOC early — in several provinces you cannot register at all without one.
fundingPage.arrive2: Check the new province’s model above. If you move from a grant province to a supplies-in-kind one, you stop buying at retail entirely.
fundingPage.arrive3: Expect a waiting period, and budget for it.
fundingPage.closingHeading: Money should not be the reason you ration supplies
fundingPage.closingBody: If the numbers are not working, that is worth saying out loud to your care team. There are usually more routes than people realise.

faq.label: Frequently asked questions
faq.heading: Questions, answered with sources.
faq.note: Practical notes, not medical advice. Each answer lists where it comes from.

1.q: Can I order my supplies here, and will my plan pay?
1.a: You can order diabetes supplies such as meters, strips, lancets, pen needles, sensors and pump supplies from the shelf. Liivv’s pharmacies serve all of Canada, Quebec and the territories included, but insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec. To fill a prescription, send it from <link>your account’s Pharmacy page</link>: choose Add prescription, then transfer it from your current pharmacy or ask your doctor to fax it. What’s covered for pumps, sensors, strips and needles is different in each province and territory, and Diabetes Canada <link>compares them by province and territory</link>. Coverage changes, so check the date on each comparison and confirm with your provincial or territorial plan. Our pharmacy in your province bills your provincial drug plan directly for what it covers, except in Quebec, where orders are paid for privately. Other programs each pay their own way: where one pays you back, we can give you an invoice for your claim. Check how yours pays before you order, or ask Liivv’s Certified Diabetes Educators.

2.a: On Diabetes Care pages, on diabetes product pages, and in a cart with diabetes supplies, we turn off advertising signals. What you read and buy there isn’t used for ads or to build ad audiences. The page address and title are left out of our site analytics, and so are the names of diabetes products.

3.q: What if a sensor stops working or comes off early?
3.a: A sensor can be up to 15 minutes slower than a finger-prick check to show your blood sugar, so keep a meter and strips as a backup, where you can reach them. Liivv’s Certified Diabetes Educators can help with sensor and supply questions: <link>call 1-844-561-1254</link>, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, except holidays. If someone can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure, <link>call 911</link>. For a low, a high or a sick day, go to <link>Staying Safe</link>.

4.q: Where do used needles, lancets and sensor applicators go?
4.a: Into a sharps container. In Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, the Health Products Stewardship Association (HPSA) gives out free sharps containers at participating collection locations, such as pharmacies. When yours is full, seal it and return it to a drop-off location. Its program takes lancets, pen tips (pen needles), syringes, infusion sets and sensor (CGM) applicators with needles. It doesn’t take glucose meters. Never put used sharps in the garbage or the recycling. Elsewhere in Canada, ask your pharmacy: many pharmacies supply safe, puncture-proof containers.

5.a: Yes. Insulin is listed in the shop. A pharmacist reviews and dispenses every insulin and glucagon order, shipped in plain packaging. Insulin is shipped cold-chain. Insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec. Your health-care team works with you to decide on your insulin and how you take it, and we don’t give dosing advice. Storage is different for each insulin. Follow its product information, or ask your pharmacist.

fundingPage.title: What your province covers for diabetes
fundingPage.lead: Help with the cost of pumps, sensors, strips and medicines depends on where you live, your type of diabetes and how you manage it. Start with your province, then add what applies to you.
fundingPage.focus: Pump and sensor programs, test strips and supplies, national pharmacare, federal programs, and the Disability Tax Credit.
fundingPage.vibe: Plain and specific. Every program links to the official page it came from, with the date we last checked it.
fundingPage.payingIntro: Some programs pay a pharmacy or a supplier. Others pay you back, or pay you a set amount. Here’s how that works when you order from us.
fundingPage.directBody: Our pharmacy in your province bills your provincial drug plan directly for what the plan covers. Each Liivv pharmacy is enrolled with its own province’s plan:
fundingPage.directQuebec: Not in Quebec: Quebec’s public drug plan generally doesn’t cover prescription drugs bought outside Quebec, so orders shipped to Quebec are paid for privately. Insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec.
fundingPage.directOther: Federal programs, territorial plans and private insurers aren’t on this list. For those, check how each one pays, or ask us.
fundingPage.claimBody: Some programs pay you back when you send them a receipt. Some pay you a set amount instead: Ontario’s Assistive Devices Program pays up to $2,400 a year toward pump supplies, sent to you as $600 every 3 months, and you buy the supplies yourself. Others pay only a pharmacy or supplier directly, so a receipt from us won’t work for them.
fundingPage.claimCheck: Paying for an order yourself and claiming it back? Ask us for an invoice for your claim. We can’t promise that a program will accept a claim, so check its rules before you order.
fundingPage.payLaterBody: For insulin pump supplies, Omnipod pods included, you can pay after you receive your order instead of when you place it. Our customer service team checks that you’re eligible first.

payLaterTerms.1: Start with three orders in a row, paid as usual.
payLaterTerms.2: Then accept the program’s terms with a $1.00 authorization on your credit card. There’s no credit check.
payLaterTerms.3: Pay for each order within 45 days of receiving it, or with your next order, whichever comes first.
payLaterTerms.4: Omnipod pod orders are billed to your card every 90 days.
payLaterTerms.5: If your card is declined, we try it 3 more times. After that, the balance is due within 3 business days. Prepaid cards can’t be used.
payLaterTerms.6: A late payment can hold up your next shipment and end your place in the program.

fundingPage.payLaterContact: To ask about it, contact Liivv. We’ll pass your question to the right team.

changes.1: April 1, 2024: Northwest Territories Extended Health Benefits became based on income rather than on a list of diseases.
changes.2: October 10, 2024: the federal Pharmacare Act became law.
changes.3: February 27 to March 20, 2025: Manitoba, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Yukon signed national pharmacare agreements.
changes.4: April 15, 2025: Manitoba made most diabetes medicines free, with no deductible.
changes.5: September 2025: Non-Insured Health Benefits added FreeStyle Libre 3, with prior approval.
changes.6: May 2025: Newfoundland and Labrador announced that its sensor program would open to everyone with type 1 who meets its criteria, from fall 2025.
changes.7: March 1, 2026: British Columbia made insulin and a set list of diabetes medicines free. Wider device and supply coverage followed on April 1.
changes.8: July 31 and November 28, 2025: the Ontario Drug Benefit began covering Dexcom G7, then FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus, for people who take insulin.
changes.9: February 4, 2026: Quebec set the same criteria for every continuous glucose monitor on its public plan’s list of exception drugs.
changes.10: October 1, 2026: Alberta’s government-sponsored drug programs began paying only after private or workplace insurance.

fundingPage.whereHeading: Ordering from Quebec or the territories
fundingPage.whereBody: Liivv’s pharmacies serve all of Canada, Quebec and the territories included. Insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec. Quebec’s public drug plan generally doesn’t cover prescription drugs bought outside Quebec, so orders shipped to Quebec are paid for privately. In Yukon, the Northwest Territories or Nunavut, you pay for your order yourself: check with your program that it will pay you back, and ask us for an invoice for your claim. Yukon’s Chronic Disease and Disability Benefits Program, for example, needs its approval before you buy outside Yukon, or a claim within 1 year.

new-to-the-journey.heroBody: Just been told, or getting set up: calm first steps, the numbers your team will talk about, and who to ask.

categoriesIntro.heading: You don’t have to learn it all at once
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter covers the first days after a diagnosis, then getting set up. If you’ve just been told, start at the top. If you already have a plan and supplies, start at Do I need a meter?

startHere.heading: Just been told, or setting up?

1.title: Just been told

items.1: There’s no right way to feel about this news, and no need to take it all in at once
items.2: Depression is more common in people with diabetes, so looking after your mood is part of looking after your diabetes
items.3: Canadian guidelines say diabetes teams should ask everyone, from time to time, about diabetes distress and about mood and anxiety. You can bring it up first
items.4: Your team will start with what you need to know first. The rest can wait

1.note: If it isn’t easing, tell your diabetes team or your doctor. If you’d like to talk to a mental health professional, Breakthrough T1D keeps a Mental Health + Diabetes Directory of registered providers.

figure.body: If you’re thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time of day or night. If your safety is at risk right now, call 911.

1.prompt: If it isn’t easing, or it’s hard to get through the day

2.prompt: If you’d like to talk to a mental health professional
2.detail: Breakthrough T1D keeps a Mental Health + Diabetes Directory of registered mental health providers.

2.title: Which diabetes is this?

items.1: Type 1: the pancreas doesn’t make insulin. 5 to 10% of people with diabetes have type 1, and it can start in adulthood too
items.2: Type 2: the most common type, 90 to 95% of people with diabetes. It may have no symptoms
items.3: Gestational diabetes: shows up during pregnancy, in 3 to 20% of pregnancies. It usually goes away after the birth, but it raises the chance of type 2 later, for you and your child
items.4: Prediabetes: blood sugar that’s higher than normal, but not yet high enough to be called type 2 diabetes
items.5: Less common types: there are less common forms, such as LADA (counted as type 1 in Canada) and monogenic diabetes, and some cases are hard to classify. If your type doesn’t seem to fit, ask your team

2.note: Know Your Type has a card for each one, including the less common types.

3.title: Your target ranges

items.1: The usual targets in Canada are 4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L before meals and 5.0 to 10.0 two hours after eating
items.2: If your A1C isn’t at target, your team may set a lower after-meal target, 5.0 to 8.0, weighing it against the risk of lows
items.3: A1C is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months. It’s usually done about every 3 months, and the usual target in Canada is 7.0% or less
items.4: If you use a sensor, Canadian guidelines use the international targets: for most adults, more than 70% of the day between 3.9 and 10.0
items.5: Your team may set different targets, for example for children, or if you’re pregnant, frail, or often have severe lows

3.note: Write your own targets on the card and keep it with your meter. If your team gave you different numbers, use theirs.

ruler.heading: Usual targets in Canada, in mmol/L
ruler.lowLink: What to do about a low: The Rule of 15
ruler.teamNote: Your team may set different numbers, for example for a child. Use theirs.

fields.4: Time in range, if I use a sensor

4.title: Food and movement: first steps

items.1: Canada’s food guide suggests plenty of vegetables and fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with plant protein more often
items.2: It suggests water as your drink of choice, and limiting highly processed foods
items.3: Canadian guidelines support more than one way of eating, including Mediterranean, DASH and vegetarian. A dietitian can help you find what fits
items.4: Start slowly, with 5 to 10 minutes of activity a day, and build up
items.5: Try to work up to 150 minutes a week of moderate to vigorous activity, such as 30 minutes on 5 days
items.6: If you haven’t been active for a while, talk to your doctor before you start anything harder than a brisk walk
items.7: If you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar, carry fast-acting sugar when you’re active

4.note: Carb counting, eating out and more on moving your body are in Everyday Liivving. If you take insulin, ask your team how to plan around activity.

5.title: Supporting someone newly diagnosed

items.1: Ask what help they’d like. Some people want company at appointments, and some would rather manage on their own
items.2: Learn what a low looks like for them, and where they keep fast-acting sugar. The steps are in <link>The Rule of 15</link>, in Staying Safe
items.3: If they’re at risk of a severe low, such as people who take insulin, Canadian guidelines say the people around them should be taught to call 911, and how to give glucagon. The signs that need emergency care are in Staying Safe
items.4: If they have type 1, immediate family aged 2 to 45, and other relatives aged 2 to 20, can ask about free research screening through TrialNet, anywhere in Canada. The details are in <link>Type 1 starts before symptoms</link>, in Know Your Type
items.5: Your own feelings count too. If you’re caring for a child or teen with type 1, Breakthrough T1D has a Caregiver Guide

5.note: More for families and caregivers is in This Might Be You.

2.heading: If they’re at risk of a severe low

6.title: Do I need a meter?

items.1: Whether you check your blood sugar at home, and how often, depends on your type and your treatment. Your team will tell you what you need
items.2: If you take insulin more than once a day, Canadian guidelines suggest checking at least 3 times a day
items.3: For type 1 on injections or a pump, Canadian guidelines recommend a sensor that reads all the time (a continuous glucose monitor). Ask your team whether that fits you
items.4: A sensor can run up to 15 minutes behind your blood sugar, so keep a meter and strips as a backup
items.5: Choosing a meter, and the strips and lancets that go with it, is in Your Tools

6.note: Some provinces cover strips and sensors, and how much often depends on your treatment. <link>Funding & Coverage</link> has the details for your province.

7.title: Your medicines and your pharmacist

items.1: What is each of my medicines for, and when do I take it?
items.2: Can any of them cause a low? If so, what should I keep with me?
items.3: Do any of them need to be paused on a sick day? The sick-day plan in Staying Safe has a space for your pharmacist to write this down
items.4: How do I store each one, and how long does it keep once it’s open?
items.5: Which supplies go with my medicines, and are they covered by my plan?

7.note: Take this list to your pharmacist or your next appointment, with your medicines or a list of them. Your prescriber chooses your medicines. Your pharmacist helps you use them safely.

8.title: Starting insulin

items.1: Everyone with type 1, and many people with type 2, need insulin to stay healthy
items.2: There’s no one-size-fits-all plan. Your team works out with you how many injections, when, how much, and whether a pump suits you
items.3: Insulin can be taken with a pen, a syringe or a pump. Pens come with an instruction book, so read it to learn how yours works
items.4: Change where you inject each time. This helps prevent fatty lumps that can make insulin work poorly
items.5: Use a new pen tip or needle every time, then put it in a sharps container
items.6: Insulin raises your risk of a low. Always have fast-acting sugar with you, at home and when you go out. The steps are in <link>The Rule of 15</link>, in Staying Safe
items.7: Storage is different for each insulin. Follow the leaflet that came with yours, or ask your pharmacist
items.8: Throw out insulin that has been frozen, has been in temperatures over 30°C, or has expired

8.note: Your prescriber chooses your insulin, and fine-tuning your routine takes time. A step-by-step injection guide is in Your Tools.

9.title: Sharps from day one

items.1: Used lancets, pen tips and needles go in a sharps container. Pen tips and needles are for one use only
items.2: Sharps include lancets, pen needles, sensor applicators that have a needle, infusion sets and syringes
items.3: Never put used sharps in the garbage or recycling
items.4: In Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, participating pharmacies give out free sharps containers and take them back
items.5: Elsewhere in Canada, ask your pharmacy. Many pharmacies supply containers and swap a full one for a new one

9.note: Ask your pharmacy where to return a full container near you.

10.title: Your starter supply list

items.1: If you check with a meter: the meter, its strips and lancets, and a sharps container
items.2: If you take insulin: a new pen tip or needle for each injection, and a sharps container
items.3: If you take insulin: fast-acting sugar with you, at home and when you go out
items.4: A card in your wallet that says you have diabetes, or medical ID such as a bracelet or necklace
items.5: If you use a sensor: a meter and strips as a backup
items.6: If you use a pump: backup insulin pens or syringes, extra pump supplies, ketone strips or a blood ketone meter, and a written copy of your pump settings

10.note: Your team’s list comes first. Ask them whether you need ketone strips or glucagon.

11.title: Who to ask

items.1: Your diabetes educator: your plan, your readings and everyday questions. Many are Certified Diabetes Educators (CDE®), licensed health professionals certified in diabetes education
items.2: Your doctor: your diagnosis, your prescriptions and your checkups
items.3: A pharmacist: what each medicine is for, how to store it, and your sick-day medicine plan
items.4: How you’re feeling: your team, or a registered mental health provider from Breakthrough T1D’s Mental Health + Diabetes Directory

11.note: Not sure where to start? Start with your diabetes educator. Some educators in the CDE directory see people without a referral.

1.heading: Learning the basics
1.body: The first months are for learning, at your own pace. Your diabetes educator can go over your plan, your readings and your questions. With gestational diabetes or prediabetes, your checkups are different, so ask your team which of these apply.

1.label: Find a CDE — Canadian Diabetes Educator Certification Board

2.heading: About every 3 months: A1C
2.body: Canadian guidelines suggest an A1C test about every 3 months. For adults whose numbers have been steady at target, your team may space it out. Your usual target is in Your target ranges.

3.heading: Eyes
3.body: Have an eye exam once a year, unless your eye-care professional suggests something different. With type 2, the first one is at diagnosis. With type 1, for people 15 and over, they start 5 years after diagnosis. Children have their own schedule. Your team tells you when yours is due.

4.heading: Kidneys
4.body: Two tests, called ACR and eGFR, check your kidneys at least once a year. With type 2 they start at diagnosis. With type 1 they usually start 5 years after diagnosis. Children have their own schedule, so ask your team.

5.heading: Feet
5.body: Wash, dry and check your feet every day, with a mirror if you need one. At least once a year, your team checks your bare feet, including feeling and blood flow.

pharmacist.heading: Questions about your first supplies
pharmacist.body: Liivv’s Certified Diabetes Educators answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to Liivv’s pharmacy in your province. Your plan and your medicines still belong with your diabetes team.

closing.heading: One step, then the next
closing.body: New to the Journey is permission to learn slowly: a few numbers, a few supplies, and people to ask.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for care from your diabetes team, doctor or pharmacist. Your type, your targets and your medicines depend on you. Your team sets them.

staying-safe.title: Staying Safe
staying-safe.heroBody: Lows, highs, ketones and sick days: what to check, what to do, and when to call. Short enough to use in a hurry.
staying-safe.focus: When you’re low: the levels, the Rule of 15, glucagon, lows that come later, and what to carry. When you’re high or sick: highs, ketones, sick days, an unexplained high on a pump, an emergency kit, and who to call.
staying-safe.vibe: Calm and practical: clear steps for the moments that matter.

categoriesIntro.heading: Your plan, in one place
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter helps you follow the plan your diabetes team made with you, and shows when it’s time to call. If your team gave you different numbers, use theirs.

urgent.heading: Get emergency care now
urgent.intro: Everyday lows and highs follow your plan. These don’t. Get emergency care now if the person:
urgent.action: Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

signs.1: Can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure. Call 911, give glucagon if you have it, turn them on their side and stay with them. Don’t put food or drink in their mouth
signs.2: Is vomiting and can’t keep fluids down
signs.3: Has blood ketones above 3.0 mmol/L, or large ketones in their urine (ranges written for type 1 diabetes)
signs.4: Has deep or hard breathing or fruity-smelling breath, or is very sleepy or confused with a high blood sugar or ketones. In pregnancy, or with some diabetes medicines, DKA can happen even when blood sugar is near normal

startHere.heading: Is your number low, or high?

1.title: Know your low

items.1: A blood sugar below 3.9 mmol/L is low
items.2: Level 1: below 3.9, down to 3.0
items.3: Level 2: below 3.0
items.4: Level 3: a low at any number where you need someone else’s help to treat it
items.5: If you use a sensor, Canadian targets for most people aim for less than 4% of the day below 3.9

1.note: Some Canadian guidance for driving and for school uses 4.0 instead of 3.9. If your team gave you a number, use theirs.

2.title: The Rule of 15

items.1: Take 15 g of fast-acting sugar
items.2: Wait 15 minutes, then check your blood sugar again
items.3: If it’s still below 3.9, take another 15 g
items.4: Once it’s back up, if your next meal is more than an hour away, have a snack with a starch and a protein

2.note: After a low, anyone who drives, teens included, should wait at least 40 minutes, and until their blood sugar is at least 5.0, before driving. More on driving in Everyday Liivving.

figure.optionsHeading: 15 g of fast-acting sugar is one of these:

options.1: Glucose tablets that add up to 15 g
options.2: ⅔ cup (150 mL) of juice or regular pop
options.4: 1 tablespoon of sugar dissolved in water

figure.childNote: From Canadian guidelines for children with type 1 diabetes who use injections, or a pump that doesn’t adjust insulin on its own. Children on an automated (closed-loop) system may need less. If your child has another type of diabetes, or uses an automated system, ask their team how much to give.

childSteps.1: Give the amount for their age
childSteps.4: Still below 3.9? Give that amount again

childItems.1: Give fast-acting sugar. The amount for the child’s age is in the table
childItems.2: Wait 15 minutes, then check their blood sugar again
childItems.3: If it’s still below 3.9, give the amount in the table again
childItems.4: Once it’s back up, if their next meal is more than an hour away, give them a snack with a starch and a protein

figure.childOptionsHeading: Each of these is 15 g of fast-acting sugar. For a child, give the amount in the table for their age:
figure.childOptionsNote: Honey isn’t on the list for children. Never give any honey to babies under 1 year.
figure.aidNote: On an automated (closed-loop) insulin system? Canadian guidelines for type 1 say people of any age may treat a low they can manage themselves with less, 5 to 10 g. Ask your team what to use.

3.title: Glucagon: help someone else gives

items.1: Glucagon is for a low when the person can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure. Someone else gives it
items.2: It comes as a nasal spray or an injection. Your pharmacist can tell you which is available
items.3: Call 911, or have someone call. Give glucagon, turn the person on their side and stay with them. Don’t put food or drink in their mouth
items.4: If a low is affecting the person’s thinking or movement but they can still swallow, give 20 g of fast-acting sugar
items.5: At school, staff named in the student’s care plan, and trained, give glucagon when the plan includes consent for it

3.note: Ask your pharmacist to show you how your glucagon works, and check its expiry date from time to time. For a child under 4, ask your child’s team which glucagon to keep.

4.title: Lows that sneak up

items.1: Exercise can keep lowering your blood sugar for up to 48 hours afterwards
items.2: Check your blood sugar regularly, especially if you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar
items.3: If you take insulin or some diabetes pills, alcohol can cause a low up to 24 hours after you drink
items.4: Eat some carbohydrate when you drink, and check your blood sugar before bed
items.5: Make sure someone with you knows to call 911 if you pass out, and to give you glucagon if you have it. Glucagon may not work as well if you’ve had more than 2 standard drinks in the past few hours, so the 911 call matters even more
items.6: A sensor can run up to 15 minutes behind your blood sugar. Keep a meter as a backup

4.note: Ask your team how to plan your medicines around exercise and drinking.

items.1: Carry fast-acting sugar when you’re active
items.2: If you have glucagon, show the people you spend time with how it works. Canadian guidelines say they should be taught
items.3: Wear medical ID, such as a bracelet or necklace
items.4: For a child at school, a care plan made before the school year covers daily care and emergencies, with at least two trained staff
items.5: Treat a student’s low right away, where it happens, and don’t leave them alone
items.6: Students may carry a phone or smartwatch to help manage their blood sugar

6.title: Highs

items.1: The usual targets in Canada are 4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L before meals and 5.0 to 10.0 two hours after meals. Your team may set different ones
items.2: Symptoms of a high can show up when your fasting blood sugar is 11 or higher
items.3: If your blood sugar stays above 14 before meals for more than a few meals, check for ketones
items.4: Ketones can build up even when blood sugar is close to normal, for example in pregnancy or with a type of diabetes pill called an SGLT2 inhibitor. Ask your pharmacist whether any of your pills is, or contains, one

6.note: Very high blood sugar or high ketones need care right away. The signs are at the top of this page.

7.title: Ketones: check and act

items.1: Ketones build up when your body doesn’t have enough insulin and starts breaking down fat for energy
items.2: You can check ketones in your blood or in your urine. Your team will tell you which to use
items.3: Check when your blood sugar stays high. With type 1, check when you’re sick too, especially with vomiting, stomach pain or a fever. With other types, check when you’re sick if your team has told you to
items.4: With type 1, Canadian guidelines say to put off hard exercise if blood ketones are 1.5 or higher
items.5: Signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) include thirst, passing a lot of urine, stomach pain, feeling or being sick, deeper breathing, fruity-smelling breath, and feeling tired, sleepy or confused. DKA needs medical care right away

7.note: The ladder below was written for type 1 diabetes. If you have another type, ask your team which numbers to use. With any type, high ketones need medical care right away.

figure.writtenFor: Written for type 1 diabetes, adapted from Breakthrough T1D

2.action: Keep checking. If you’re sick, call your diabetes team

3.action: Risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Call your team now. If you can’t reach them, go to the emergency department

4.action: Medical emergency. Get emergency care now

2.action: Risk of DKA. Call your team now. If you can’t reach them, go to the emergency department

3.action: Medical emergency. Get emergency care now

8.title: Sick days

items.1: These sick-day steps are for vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or a lot of heat or humidity without enough to drink: anything that can leave you dehydrated
Drink plenty of fluids with little sugar, unless you’ve been told to limit fluids
items.2: If you can’t eat, have foods with 15 g of carbohydrate instead. The sick-day sheet under Sources lists some
items.3: If you use insulin, keep taking it when you’re sick. Check your blood sugar more often. Your insulin may need adjusting, so ask your team how

items.1: Some medicines are stopped for a short time if you’re eating less, or dehydrated, for more than 24 hours. The sick-day sheet under Sources lists them
items.2: Which of your own medicines this means is a question for your pharmacist. The plan on this card has a space for them to write it down
items.3: Restart them once you’re eating and drinking normally

items.1: Vomiting and can’t keep fluids down: go to the emergency department. If you can reach your team right away, call them too
items.2: If you’re sick and can’t eat, call your doctor or go to the emergency department if you vomit or have diarrhea 2 or more times in 4 hours
items.3: Call your team or go to the emergency department if you can’t drink enough, don’t know which medicines to stop or how to adjust your insulin, or your ketones are moderate. Large ketones need emergency care now
items.4: Do the same if vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, passing a lot of urine, extreme thirst, weakness or fever isn’t getting better. Trouble breathing needs emergency care now

8.note: Fill in the plan on this card with your pharmacist and diabetes team before you’re sick, so it’s ready when you need it.

fields.2: How often to check my blood sugar when I’m sick
fields.3: When to check ketones, and blood or urine
fields.4: My medicines to pause, and when to restart them (filled in with my pharmacist)
fields.5: Foods and drinks I can manage when I’m sick

9.title: On a pump: an unexplained high

items.1: Keep backup supplies, such as rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes, and learn how to switch to injections in case you can’t use your pump
items.2: If your blood sugar is high and you can’t explain it, check your ketones and follow the ladder in Ketones: check and act
items.3: Keep a written copy of your pump settings in your emergency kit

9.note: Your pump team’s plan comes first. Ask them what to do if you think your pump has stopped giving insulin.

items.1: Keep an emergency kit with at least one to two weeks of supplies
items.2: Include fast-acting sugar, glucagon if you have it, ketone strips and a sharps container
items.3: If you use a pump, add a written copy of your settings
items.4: Keep unopened insulin in the fridge, at 2 to 8 °C. Throw out insulin that has frozen, been above 30 °C, or expired
items.5: How long an opened pen or vial lasts depends on the product. Most are good for up to 28 days once opened, and some for longer. Follow the leaflet that came with your insulin

items.1: 911: someone can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure
items.2: Emergency department, or 911: blood ketones over 3.0, large urine ketones, vomiting with no fluids kept down, or signs of DKA such as deep breathing or fruity-smelling breath
items.3: Your diabetes team, now: blood ketones 1.5 to 3.0, or moderate urine ketones. If you can’t reach them, go to the emergency department
items.4: Your diabetes team: blood ketones 0.6 to under 1.5 when you’re sick, or small urine ketones
items.5: Your pharmacist: your sick-day medicine plan, and how your glucagon works

6.label: Liivv’s Certified Diabetes Educators
6.body: Questions about pumps, sensors, meters and other diabetes supplies, and about billing and claims.

1.heading: Treat and check again
1.body: A low: take 15 g of fast-acting sugar, wait 15 minutes and check again. Still below 3.9? Take 15 g more. For a child, the amount depends on their age: see The Rule of 15.

2.heading: Call your team
2.body: Blood ketones 0.6 to under 1.5 when you’re sick, or small urine ketones.

3.heading: Call your team now
3.body: Blood ketones 1.5 to 3.0, or moderate urine ketones. If you can’t reach your team, go to the emergency department.

4.heading: Emergency care, or 911
4.body: Can’t swallow, unconscious or having a seizure: call 911. Blood ketones over 3.0, large urine ketones, vomiting with no fluids kept down, or signs of DKA: get emergency care now.

pharmacist.heading: Questions about pumps, sensors, supplies or claims
pharmacist.body: Liivv’s Certified Diabetes Educators answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to Liivv’s pharmacy in your province. For a low or a high right now, follow your plan or the steps on this page.

closing.heading: A plan you already know
closing.body: Staying safe is the same few steps, practised: check, act, check again, and know when to call.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for care from your diabetes team, doctor or pharmacist. Your targets, your medicines and your sick-day plan depend on you. Your team sets them.

your-tools.title: Your Tools
your-tools.heroBody: Meters, sensors, pens, syringes and pumps: what each one does, what works with what, and how to use them well.
your-tools.focus: Checking your glucose: choosing a meter, the strips and lancets that go with it, sensors and what pairs with them, time in range, and when to restock. Getting insulin in: pen needles, syringes, giving an injection, moving your sites, keeping insulin safe, pumps in plain words, what fits your pump, and a backup plan.
your-tools.vibe: Practical and unhurried: know your tools, and use them with confidence.

categoriesIntro.heading: The right supplies, used well
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter explains your tools and how to use them. It doesn’t choose your treatment: your team does that with you. If your team, or the guide that came with your device, says something different, follow them.

startHere.heading: Checking your glucose, or getting insulin in?

1.title: Choosing a meter

items.1: A meter reads a drop of blood from a finger prick. The drop goes on a test strip, and the strip goes into the meter
items.2: You can get a meter at most pharmacies, or from your diabetes educator
items.3: Once you have a meter, get trained on it before you start using it
items.4: How often you check depends on your treatment plan. Your team will tell you when, and how often
items.5: Even if you use a sensor, keep a meter and strips, to double-check a reading and as a backup

1.note: Ask your pharmacist or educator which meter suits you. Coverage is under How supplies get paid for, below.

2.title: Strips, lancets and control solution that match

items.1: Ask which test strips to use with your meter, and whether your meter needs to be coded to read them
items.2: Used lancets go in a sharps container. Many pharmacies give out puncture-proof containers and swap a full one for a new one
items.3: In Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, the Health Products Stewardship Association (HPSA) gives out free sharps containers at participating collection locations, such as pharmacies
items.4: Never put sharps in the garbage or the recycling
items.5: Elsewhere in Canada, ask your pharmacy how to return used sharps

2.note: If you’re not sure a strip, lancet or control solution fits your meter, check your meter’s guide or ask your pharmacist before you use it.

figure.notConfirmed: Not confirmed here yet. Check your meter’s guide, or ask your pharmacist

3.title: Your meter lesson: questions to take in

items.1: How and where to take a drop of blood
items.2: How to use your lancets, and how to throw them away
items.3: How big a drop of blood your meter needs
items.4: Which test strips to use
items.5: How to clean your meter
items.6: How to check that your meter is accurate
items.7: How to code your meter to read your strips, if it needs it

3.note: These are good questions to ask. Fill in the lines with your pharmacist or educator, and keep the card with your meter.

4.title: Sensors: which pairs with what

items.1: A sensor sits on your skin like a small patch, held on by adhesive, with a thin filament just under the skin. It measures sugar in the fluid between your cells, so it can read your sugar without a finger prick each time
items.2: Some sensors give a reading only when you scan them with your phone. Others show your sugar all the time and can sound alarms for lows and highs
items.3: Some sensors connect to an insulin pump. That connection is what a hybrid closed-loop system needs
items.4: This technology isn’t for everyone, so talk with your team about whether it’s right for you

4.note: Makers update which devices work together. Before you switch a sensor or a pump, check with your team, your device maker or a Liivv pharmacist who is a Certified Diabetes Educator (CDE).

5.title: Wearing a sensor, and time in range

items.1: Time in range is the share of your day that your sugar stays in your target range
items.2: For most people, Canadian guidelines aim for more than 70% of the day between 3.9 and 10.0 mmol/L
items.3: They also aim for less than 4% of the day below 3.9
items.4: Going from 60% to 65% of the day in range adds about an hour a day in range
items.5: Targets can be different in pregnancy, and for children, older adults and people who have lows often. Your team sets yours
items.6: You can share your sensor readings from your phone with your diabetes team, so they can see your patterns over time
items.7: A sensor and a finger check are more likely to differ when you’re eating or exercising. If how you feel doesn’t match your sensor, or you’re treating a low, a finger check gives the most accurate number

5.note: Some Canadian sources give the range as 4.0 to 10.0. If your team gave you a range, use theirs.

6.title: Sensor restock calculator

items.1: Your sensor’s guide says how many days each sensor is worn. The calculator multiplies that by the number of sensors you have
items.2: If a program pays for your sensors, it may limit how many you get. For example, for one sensor it covers, the Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program for eligible First Nations and Inuit allows up to 14 every 6 months, with prior approval, for people who manage their diabetes with insulin
items.3: Your province or territory may set its own limits. Ask your pharmacist, or see How supplies get paid for, below

6.note: The calculator does arithmetic only. It doesn’t know your coverage, and it can’t count a sensor that stops early.

7.title: Pen needles: length and angle

items.1: An insulin pen comes filled with insulin. You put a new needle tip on for each injection
items.2: You need a separate pen for each type of insulin you use
items.3: Shorter, thinner needles are suggested, such as 4, 5 or 6 mm, so the insulin doesn’t go into muscle
items.4: For adults, a skin lift may not be needed with a 4 mm needle. Use one with a needle 8 mm or longer
items.5: Put the needle in at 90°, with a quick, smooth motion. With a longer needle, 8 or 12 mm, you may need to gently lift the skin, or go in at 45°
items.6: If there’s little fat on your arms, legs or belly, a skin lift may be needed even with a 5 or 6 mm needle

7.note: Your educator or pharmacist can show you which length suits you, and how to lift the skin if you need to.

8.title: Syringes, and insulin strength

items.1: Today’s syringes are smaller and use thinner needles. They cost less than pens and pumps
items.2: Insulin comes in more than one strength. Most is U-100 (100 units/mL). Some insulins are stronger, such as U-200, U-300, U-500 or U-700, and each of these comes in its own pen
items.3: If you use a pump, keep rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes as a backup
items.4: Flying? The Canadian Air Transport Security Authority (CATSA) says a syringe needs its needle guard on, and the insulin it’s for has to be with you
items.5: If your insulin is stronger than U-100 (the label says 200, 300, 500 or 700 units/mL), never use a syringe to take it out of the pen. A syringe can’t measure it correctly, and you could get far too much insulin and a severe low

8.note: Always carry a spare pen and needles. If your pen stops working, or you can’t use it, ask your pharmacist what to do before you use a syringe.

9.title: Giving an injection, step by step

items.1: Wash your hands with soap and water, and make sure the injection site is clean
items.2: You don’t need to wipe your skin with alcohol. If you do, let it dry completely first
items.3: Check the expiry date on your cartridge or vial
items.4: Wipe the rubber seal on the pen or vial with alcohol before you put on a new needle. Don’t wipe the needle itself
items.5: Cloudy insulin needs mixing until it looks milky white: roll it 10 times between your hands, then tip it upside down and back 10 times. Don’t shake it

items.1: Put on a new needle, then prime the pen to check the needle isn’t blocked, the way your pen’s instructions say
items.2: Dial the dose your team has set
items.3: Put the needle in at 90° with a quick, smooth motion
items.4: Press the button until the counter shows 0, or the syringe is empty. Count to 10 before you take the needle out
items.5: Put the needle straight into your sharps container. Don’t leave a needle on your pen between injections
items.6: Don’t inject through clothing

9.note: Your pen comes with an instruction book. Read it, so you know how your pen works.

10.title: Choosing and moving your sites

items.1: Change where you inject each time. This helps prevent fatty lumps that can make insulin work poorly
items.2: Insulin goes in fastest and most evenly from the belly. Stay about 5 cm (2 inches), three finger widths, from your belly button
items.3: Insulin goes in more slowly from the buttocks and thighs. The back of the upper arm is hard to reach on your own, so it’s often not suggested
items.4: Try leaving at least 1 to 2 cm, about a finger width, between injections, and splitting each area into four zones, using one zone for a week before you move on
items.5: Check and feel your injection areas regularly for lumps or dents
items.6: Avoid scars, moles and any other changes in the skin
items.7: Injecting into a part of your body you’re about to exercise can make insulin act faster and lower your sugar

10.note: If you find a lump or a dent, show it to your educator or your team.

figure.heading: One area, four zones
figure.centre: Keep about 5 cm from your belly button
figure.caption: Use one zone for a week, at least a finger width from your last injection each time. Then move to the next zone.

items.1: Keep unopened insulin in the fridge, at 2 to 8 °C
items.2: Keep the insulin you’re using at room temperature
items.3: Throw out insulin that has frozen, been above 30 °C, or expired
items.4: How long an opened pen or vial lasts depends on the product. Most are good for up to 28 days once opened, and some for longer. Follow the leaflet that came with your insulin
items.5: Check the expiry date before you open a new cartridge or vial
items.6: Insulin goes in your carry-on when you fly, not in checked luggage
items.7: CATSA lets insulin, juice and gels through security above the 100 mL limit, but you need to declare them separately

12.title: Pumps and automated insulin delivery, in plain words

items.1: An insulin pump is a small device worn outside your body. It gives insulin through a small tube under the skin, 24 hours a day
items.2: It gives a small, steady trickle of insulin between meals and overnight. Extra doses can be given when they’re needed, for food or to bring a high down
items.3: Some pumps connect to a sensor and respond to your readings. This is called a hybrid closed-loop system. You may also hear it called automated insulin delivery
items.4: For type 1 diabetes, Canadian guidelines prefer automated insulin delivery for everyone who is willing and able to wear and use the devices
items.5: Your team works with you to decide whether a pump suits you, and on your pump settings

12.note: Help with paying for a pump depends on where you live. See How supplies get paid for, below.

items.2: Makers’ Canadian sites list some of the sensors that work with their pumps. The picker shows what we could confirm, and says so where we couldn’t

14.title: Pump backup and set changes

items.1: Make a pump backup plan before you need one
items.2: Backup supplies include rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes, long-acting insulin if your team says you need it, extra infusion sets and reservoirs, and ketone strips or a blood ketone meter
items.3: Learn how to switch to injections in case you can’t use your pump, and keep a written copy of your pump settings
items.4: Used infusion sets and sensor applicators with needles go in a sharps container. HPSA’s program takes them in Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Elsewhere, ask your pharmacy

14.note: How often to change your set, and where to put it, are part of your pump training. If your sugar is high and you can’t explain it, check your ketones and follow <link>On a pump: an unexplained high</link>, in Staying Safe.

1.heading: It depends where you live
1.body: Coverage for pumps, sensors, test strips and needles is different in each province and territory. Diabetes Canada compares them side by side.

2.heading: First Nations and Inuit (NIHB)
2.body: For eligible First Nations and Inuit, the Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program covers some sensors for people who manage their diabetes with insulin. Some need prior approval. It also covers up to 800 test strips every 100 days for people who use insulin.

1.label: Non-Insured Health Benefits program updates — Indigenous Services Canada

3.heading: The disability tax credit
3.body: The Canada Revenue Agency treats type 1 diabetes as meeting its life-sustaining therapy test. You still need to apply, with form T2201 or online.

1.label: Disability tax credit: life-sustaining therapy — Canada Revenue Agency

4.heading: Your province’s programs
4.body: Funding & Coverage shows what we’ve confirmed for your province, with a link to each official page, and how paying works when you order from us.

pharmacist.heading: Questions about what fits your pump or sensor
pharmacist.body: Liivv’s Certified Diabetes Educators answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to Liivv’s pharmacy in your province. Your diabetes team decides your treatment and settings.

closing.heading: Tools you know well
closing.body: The right supplies, used the same careful way each time, make every day a little easier. When something doesn’t fit, ask.
