every-day-living.title: Everyday Liivving
every-day-living.heroBody: Food, movement, mood, travel and driving, then the checkups that look after your feet, eyes, kidneys and heart.
every-day-living.focus: Day to day: food, carb counting, being active, alcohol and cannabis, stress and sleep, flying and driving. Protecting your body: your feet, eyes, kidneys and heart, your checkup year, and your rights.
every-day-living.vibe: Practical and unhurried: how a day works, and what to check each year.

categoriesIntro.heading: Diabetes, around the rest of your life
categoriesIntro.body: The first half is the everyday: what you eat, how you move, how you feel, and getting around. The second is the checkups that find changes early. If your team gave you different targets or advice, use theirs.

1.title: Food without a rulebook

items.1: Canadian guidelines describe several styles of eating that work well with diabetes, including Mediterranean, Nordic, DASH and vegetarian
items.2: Canada’s food guide suggests plenty of vegetables, fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with protein from plants more often
items.3: Make water your drink of choice
items.4: Choose whole and less processed foods more often than sugary drinks, fast food and refined grains
items.5: Notice when you’re hungry and when you’re full
items.6: Culture and food traditions can be part of healthy eating

1.note: A registered dietitian can help you make a meal plan that fits your culture, your tastes and your blood sugar goals.

2.title: Carb counting

items.1: Canadian guidelines suggest learning to count carbohydrate, because how much you eat at one time usually matters
items.2: Your body turns carbohydrate into sugar, which raises your blood sugar. Both the kind and the amount matter
items.3: Carbohydrate is in grains and starches, fruit, some vegetables, legumes, milk and milk alternatives, sweet foods and many prepared foods. Meat and alternatives, most vegetables and fats have little
items.4: A common guide for most people is about 45 to 60 g of carbohydrate at a meal and 15 to 30 g at a snack. A dietitian or diabetes educator can help you set your own goals
items.5: Try to keep each meal and snack within 5 g of your goal
items.6: On a Nutrition Facts table, check the serving size first. Then take the total carbohydrate and subtract the fibre: 36 g of carbohydrate with 6 g of fibre counts as 30 g

2.note: If you take insulin with meals, work out with your team how carbohydrate and insulin fit together. This card covers counting only.

fields.5: Set with (my dietitian or diabetes educator)

3.title: Moving your body

items.1: Aim for at least 150 minutes a week of activity that raises your breathing and heart rate, like brisk walking, cycling, swimming or dancing
items.2: Spread it over at least 3 days, with no more than 2 days in a row off
items.3: Start slowly, with 5 to 10 minutes a day, and build up. Less than 150 minutes still has benefits
items.4: Add strength exercises at least 2 times a week, with weights, bands or your own body weight. If you’re new to them, get some instruction first
items.5: Break up long periods of sitting. Canadian guidelines suggest getting up briefly every 20 to 30 minutes
items.6: If you’ve been inactive for a while, talk to your doctor before starting anything harder than a brisk walk. If you have chest pain, pressure or discomfort, or you’re much more short of breath than usual, stop the activity and call 911 right away. These can be signs of a heart attack. Tell your doctor about it too, before you exercise again
items.7: Exercise can lower your blood sugar for up to 48 hours. If you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar, check regularly and carry fast-acting sugar. More in Staying Safe, under <link>Lows that sneak up</link>

3.note: Ask your team how to plan food and medicines around activity, especially if you use insulin.

4.title: Alcohol and cannabis

items.1: Canadian guidelines (2023) say that if you don’t drink, it’s healthier not to start. If you do drink, talk with your team about what’s right for you
items.2: Don’t drink if you’re pregnant or trying to get pregnant, breastfeeding, have a personal or family history of drinking problems, are about to drive or do anything that needs your full attention, or take certain medicines. Ask your pharmacist about yours. The 2018 sheet in this card’s Sources gives drink limits that are older than the 2023 advice on this card
items.3: If you take insulin or some other diabetes medicines, a low can come up to 24 hours after drinking. Eat carbohydrate when you drink, check your blood sugar before bed, and make sure someone with you knows how to help, including calling 911 if you pass out. More in Staying Safe, under <link>Lows that sneak up</link>
items.4: Alternating alcoholic drinks with water helps you avoid getting dehydrated
items.5: Canadian guidelines (2023) say that if you drink, cutting down lowers the risk to your health, and that this may mean no more than 2 standard drinks a week. At 2 standard drinks or fewer a week you’re likely to avoid harm from alcohol, more than 2 at one time raises the risk of harms such as injuries, and less is better. Your team can help if you want to cut down
items.6: Recreational cannabis isn’t recommended for teens or adults with diabetes. With type 1, avoid it, because it raises the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
items.7: If you do use cannabis, edibles can contain carbohydrate, and cannabis can make you hungrier. Adults who use it should be offered advice on lowering the risks

4.note: Alcohol and cannabis aren’t things to hide from your team. Your health-care providers should talk about them with you regularly, without judgement.

5.title: Distress, stress and sleep

items.1: Living with diabetes can feel like a burden. Its constant demands can lead to diabetes distress, low moods and anxiety
items.2: You may feel angry, guilty, frightened, discouraged or low. These are valid responses to a long-term condition
items.3: Depression is more common in people with diabetes, and there are effective treatments
items.4: Problems with eating, sleeping and stress are common too. Tell your team about them
items.5: So is fear of lows. If it’s holding you back, tell your team, because there are ways to help
items.6: Canadian guidelines say everyone with diabetes, and parents and caregivers of young people with diabetes, should be checked regularly for diabetes distress. Your team may give you a short questionnaire to fill in before a visit
items.7: Regular activity can lower stress and help you relax and sleep

5.note: If it isn’t easing, or you’re struggling to get through the day, tell your diabetes team or your doctor rather than waiting it out.

figure.body: If you’re thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time of day or night. If your safety is at risk right now, call 911.

1.prompt: If it isn’t easing, or you’re struggling to get through the day

2.prompt: If you’d like to talk with a mental health provider
2.detail: Run by Breakthrough T1D. It lists registered mental health providers.

6.title: Flying with diabetes supplies

items.1: Keep insulin and your supplies in your carry-on. Don’t put insulin in checked luggage, because temperature changes can damage it
items.2: Insulin, and juice or gel to treat a low, can go through security in amounts over 100 mL. Declare them to the screening officer separately
items.3: Syringes are allowed with the needle guard on, as long as you’re carrying the medicine they’re for
items.4: Pumps and sensors are allowed. Don’t wear them through the body scanner or put a pump through the X-ray machine. You can ask for a physical search instead, in private if you like
items.5: You don’t have to tell screening staff you have diabetes, and you don’t have to take off your pump. Just tell the screening officer you’re wearing one
items.6: Keep medicine in its labelled packaging. Bring a letter from your doctor and a list of your medicines from your pharmacist
items.7: Pack spare insulin and supplies. In the heat, keep insulin in an insulated bag. In the cold, keep it close to your body so it doesn’t freeze

6.note: Crossing time zones can change when you take insulin or diabetes pills. Plan it with your doctor or diabetes educator before you go.

7.title: Driving

items.1: These steps are for people who take insulin, or a diabetes pill that can cause lows
items.2: Check your blood sugar right before you drive, any time you feel low, and at least every 4 hours while driving, or wear a real-time sensor
items.3: Don’t start driving if your blood sugar is below 4.0 mmol/L
items.4: After treating a low, wait at least 40 minutes, and until your blood sugar is at least 5.0 mmol/L, before you drive
items.5: If a low starts while you’re driving, stop somewhere safe, take the keys out of the ignition and treat it. The 40-minute wait applies here too
items.6: Keep fast-acting sugar within reach of the driver’s seat, and your meter and supplies with you
items.7: If you no longer feel the early signs of a low, or you’ve had a severe low in the past year, Canadian guidelines say to check right before you drive and at least every 2 hours while driving, or wear a real-time sensor
items.8: A severe low is one where you pass out or need someone else’s help. If you have one while driving, stop driving right away. Tell your health-care provider and your driver licensing office right away, and do the same if you have more than one severe low while awake in the past 6 months (12 months for commercial drivers). Your provider may tell you not to drive
items.9: You have the right to be assessed for a driver’s licence as an individual. Licensing is handled by each province and territory. Licensing offices require a higher level of medical fitness to drive a bus, a commercial van, a transport truck or an emergency vehicle. Canadian guidelines say commercial drivers should have a medical exam when they apply for their licence

7.note: Most Canadian guidance uses 3.9 for a low, and 4.0 for driving. This card uses 4.0 because the driving guidance does. If your team gave you a number, use theirs.

3.heading: If lows are harder to spot

8.title: Your feet, every day

items.1: Diabetes can damage the nerves and blood flow in your feet, so you may not feel a blister or cut, and it can be slower to heal
items.2: Wash your feet in warm, not hot, water and dry them well, especially between the toes
items.3: Check your feet and between your toes for cuts, blisters or changes. Use a hand mirror for the soles, or ask someone to help
items.4: Put lotion on your heels and soles, but not between your toes. Trim your nails straight across, not too short
items.5: Wear clean socks and well-fitting shoes. Test bath water with your hand before you step in
items.6: Have your bare feet checked by your doctor or a foot-care specialist, such as a podiatrist, chiropodist or foot-care nurse. Ask them to check for nerve damage and blood flow too
items.7: See your doctor or a foot-care specialist right away for swelling, warmth, redness or pain in your feet or legs, or for corns, calluses, ingrown toenails, warts or slivers. Don’t treat these yourself. An open sore (a foot ulcer) or signs of infection need care right away, even if they don’t hurt. Don’t wait if a sore gets more painful, red, warm, smelly or starts to drain, if your foot is red, warm and changing shape, or if skin turns black or your legs or feet hurt at rest: see your doctor right away or go to the emergency department. A serious foot infection doesn’t always cause a fever
items.8: Don’t go barefoot, even indoors. Don’t use over-the-counter corn or wart treatments, or put hot water bottles or heating pads on your feet

8.note: If you’ve been told your feet are at high risk, you may need checks more often, and shoes fitted by a professional.

9.title: Your eyes

items.1: Diabetes can damage the small blood vessels in the retina, at the back of the eye. This is called diabetic retinopathy
items.2: It often goes unnoticed until it affects your sight, so regular exams matter even when you see well
items.3: An optometrist or ophthalmologist does the exam, often after drops that widen your pupils
items.4: Have an eye exam once a year, unless your optometrist or ophthalmologist suggests something different. With type 2, the first exam is at diagnosis. With type 1, yearly exams start 5 years after diagnosis, from age 15. For a child under 15, ask your child’s team
items.5: Canadian eye specialists also suggest an exam at least once a year. If you’re planning a pregnancy, Canadian advice differs: the diabetes guidelines say to have an exam before you get pregnant and while you’re pregnant, and eye specialists suggest one in the first trimester
items.6: See an eye doctor right away if you notice dark spots, blurred, distorted or double vision, or large floaters. If you suddenly see flashes of light with a lot of new floaters, or part of your vision goes dark, don’t wait: see an eye doctor right away, or go to the emergency department if you can’t be seen today. It can be a sign of a torn or detached retina
items.7: Found early, retinopathy can often be treated successfully, and treatment can keep your sight from getting worse. Sight that has already been lost can’t be restored, which is why early exams matter
items.8: Keeping your blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol in range helps protect your eyes

9.note: If an exam finds little or no damage, Canadian guidelines allow 1 to 2 years between exams with type 2. Your eye-care professional and diabetes team decide your schedule, and can share your results with each other.

10.title: Your kidneys

items.1: Diabetes is the leading cause of kidney disease in Canada. Up to half of people with diabetes will have signs of kidney damage in their lifetime
items.2: Good diabetes management and regular screening can prevent or delay the loss of kidney function
items.3: Most people have no symptoms early on, so screening is how kidney disease is found
items.4: Screening is two tests: a urine test (ACR) that looks for protein, and a blood test (eGFR) that shows how well your kidneys are working
items.5: With type 2, screening starts at diagnosis. With type 1, it starts 5 years after diagnosis. After that, it’s once a year
items.6: Keeping your blood sugar and blood pressure at target, not smoking, and taking your medicines as prescribed all help protect your kidneys
items.7: If you have kidney disease, a dietitian can tell you whether to change how much protein, potassium, phosphate or salt you eat
items.8: Some diabetes medicines also help protect the kidneys and heart. Ask your team whether yours does, and don’t change a medicine on your own

10.note: Ask your team for your ACR and eGFR results, and what they mean for you. Children follow their own schedule, so ask your child’s team.

11.title: Your heart: the ABCDEs

items.1: Diabetes raises the risk of heart disease and stroke. Heart disease may come 15 years earlier than in people without diabetes
items.2: You can lower that risk considerably by working on all your risk factors with your team. They’re often summed up as the ABCDEs
items.3: A1C is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar over time. Most people aim for 7% or less
items.4: Most people aim for a blood pressure below 130/80
items.5: The usual LDL (“bad”) cholesterol target is below 2.0 mmol/L
items.6: Some medicines protect the heart. Ask your team whether any are right for you
items.7: Regular physical activity and healthy eating
items.8: Screening for complications in your heart, feet, kidneys and eyes; stopping smoking, with help if you want it; and self-management, including handling stress
items.9: Have your blood pressure checked at every diabetes visit, your A1C every 3 months, and your cholesterol every year, or more often if you take medicine to lower it

11.note: Your targets are yours to set with your team. A1C targets are different in pregnancy, for older adults and for children 12 and under.

4.heading: D · Drugs to protect your heart

12.title: Work and your rights

items.1: People with diabetes should be eligible for any job they’re qualified for
items.2: People with diabetes should have the right to look after their diabetes in public places
items.3: People with diabetes have the right to care that supports the best quality of life wherever they are, including in hospital and long-term care
items.4: For a driver’s licence, you have the right to be assessed as an individual. More in <link>Driving</link>
items.5: Coverage for medicines, supplies and devices varies across Canada, and you may be eligible for the Disability Tax Credit
items.6: Diabetes Canada’s information and support line is 1-800-226-8464

12.note: Position statements on employment, insurance and self-care in public places are linked from the rights page in this card’s Sources.

1.heading: Eyes
1.body: Once a year, unless your eye-care professional suggests something different. Type 2: the first exam at diagnosis. Type 1: from age 15, starting 5 years after diagnosis. For a child under 15, ask your child’s team. See Your eyes.

2.heading: Kidneys
2.body: A urine test (ACR) and a blood test (eGFR) once a year: from diagnosis with type 2, and from 5 years after diagnosis with type 1. See Your kidneys.

3.heading: Feet
3.body: A bare-foot check by your doctor or a foot-care specialist at least once a year, including nerves and blood flow, and more often if you’re at high risk. In between, check them yourself every day: see Your feet, every day.

4.heading: Heart
4.body: Blood pressure at every diabetes visit, A1C about every 3 months or as your team advises, and cholesterol once a year. See Your heart: the ABCDEs.

1.title: 9-8-8: call or text, any time
1.body: If you are thinking about suicide, or worried about someone who is. Free, 24/7, in English and French. If your safety is at risk, call 911.

2.title: Taking care of your mental health
2.body: Diabetes distress, low moods and anxiety, and when to reach out to your health-care team.

3.title: Mental health support
3.body: A directory with information about registered mental health providers, and a guide for parents and caregivers of children and teens with type 1.

1.title: Diabetic supplies
1.body: What airport security allows. Insulin, juice and gels can go over 100 mL; declare them to the screening officer.

2.title: Air travel
2.body: Insulin in your carry-on, pumps and sensors at screening, and what to pack.

3.title: Trips
3.body: Planning a trip, and buying travel insurance.

1.title: The rights of people living with diabetes
1.body: At work, in public, and in hospital and long-term care.

2.title: Human rights complaints
2.body: For discrimination by a federally regulated employer or service. The Commission also helps you work out where to go instead, such as your province’s or territory’s human rights commission.

1.title: Virtual Diabetes Education Program
1.body: Free live online sessions led by registered health professionals, for people newly diagnosed or wanting a refresher.

2.title: InfoDiabetes Service
2.body: Questions about diabetes, answered by Diabetes Québec’s health professionals by phone, email or chat. Not an emergency service: for an emergency, call 911.

pharmacist.heading: Travelling with a pump or sensor?
pharmacist.body: Liivv’s Certified Diabetes Educators answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to Liivv’s pharmacy in your province. Your targets, your medicines and your checkups belong with your diabetes team.

closing.heading: A life, not a list
closing.body: Most of this becomes routine: a look at your feet, some movement most days, a few checkups a year. The rest is knowing who to ask.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for care from your diabetes team, doctor or pharmacist. Your targets, your medicines and your checkup schedule depend on you. Your team sets them.

know-your-type.title: Know Your Type
know-your-type.heroBody: The common types of diabetes, the less common ones, and the clues that your type might be different. Your team decides your type. This chapter helps you ask.
know-your-type.focus: The common types: type 1 at any age, type 2, prediabetes, gestational diabetes, and how type 1 starts before symptoms. Less common types: when your type might be different, LADA, MODY, diabetes in babies, genetic syndromes, pancreas conditions and iron overload, cystic fibrosis-related diabetes, and diabetes from medicines or after a transplant.
know-your-type.vibe: Clear and curious: what each type is, and the right questions to ask.

categoriesIntro.heading: What your type means
categoriesIntro.body: Most people have one of the common types. Some have a less common type, and for some the type becomes clearer over time. This chapter explains each one, and the clues worth raising with your team. Your team decides your type.

startHere.heading: One of the common types, or something less common?

1.title: Type 1, including in adults

items.1: 5 to 10% of people with diabetes have type 1. In type 1, the pancreas makes no insulin, so insulin is taken by injection or with a pump
items.2: Type 1 can start in adulthood. An estimated 71% of people with type 1 in Canada were diagnosed as adults
items.3: 85% have no family connection to type 1
items.4: Signs your team looks for include type 1 antibodies in the blood, very little insulin of your own (a low C-peptide), and a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
items.5: For type 1, Canadian guidelines name automated insulin delivery as the preferred option for anyone willing and able to use it. Otherwise, they recommend a sensor (CGM) with a pump or with injections

1.note: <link>Ketones and DKA</link> are covered in Staying Safe. The test names are explained in Could my type be different?

2.title: Type 2

items.1: Type 2 is the most common type. 90 to 95% of people with diabetes have it
items.2: Risk factors include being over 40, having diabetes in your family, and your ethnic background. Type 2 may cause no symptoms
items.3: In Canada, diabetes is diagnosed with any one of these results:
items.4: A fasting blood sugar of 7.0 mmol/L or higher
items.5: An A1C of 6.5% or higher, in adults. It isn’t used when type 1 is suspected
items.6: A blood sugar of 11.1 mmol/L or higher, 2 hours after a glucose drink or at any time of day
items.7: Without symptoms, a second test on another day confirms it
items.8: With symptoms of high blood sugar, the diagnosis is made without a second test, and treatment shouldn’t be delayed. Contact your doctor or another health-care provider today, without waiting for a second test. <link>Emergency signs</link> are in Staying Safe
items.9: For children and teens with type 2, antibody testing should be considered, because up to 10 to 20% test positive

2.note: If your diabetes doesn’t fit the usual picture, see Could my type be different?

3.title: Prediabetes

items.1: Prediabetes means a blood sugar above the usual range, but below the numbers for diabetes. In Canada, any one of these results is used:
items.2: A fasting blood sugar of 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L
items.3: An A1C of 6.0 to 6.4%
items.4: A blood sugar of 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L, 2 hours after a glucose drink
items.5: Diabetes Canada’s Prediabetes page links to the CANRISK test
items.6: Not everyone with prediabetes goes on to develop type 2, but many people do

3.note: Ask your doctor what your numbers mean for you, and when to test again.

4.title: Gestational, or diabetes from before pregnancy?

items.1: Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar first found during pregnancy. Diabetes from before pregnancy, type 1 or type 2, was diagnosed before you conceived
items.2: Diabetes that is clearly there early in pregnancy is counted on its own, as overt diabetes, not as gestational diabetes
items.3: If you’re at high risk, Canadian guidelines include an A1C test before 20 weeks
items.4: Screening for gestational diabetes is offered between 24 and 28 weeks
items.5: Gestational diabetes affects 3 to 20% of pregnancies and usually goes away after birth. It raises the chance of type 2 and heart disease later
items.6: After the birth, a glucose tolerance test between 6 weeks and 6 months is recommended
items.7: International guidance says a steady fasting blood sugar of 5.5 to 8 mmol/L, with diabetes in the family, can point to a single-gene type called GCK-MODY. If that sounds like you, tell your team early in pregnancy

4.note: Fill in the reminder with your team before the birth. Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2 is covered in This Might Be You.

fields.2: My glucose tolerance test, between 6 weeks and 6 months after the birth, is booked for
fields.3: Who orders it, and where I go

5.title: Type 1 starts before symptoms

items.1: Type 1 starts before there are symptoms. Stages 1 and 2 come before diagnosis, and international guidance defines the stages like this:
items.2: Stage 1: two or more type 1 antibodies, with normal blood sugar
items.3: Stage 2: two or more type 1 antibodies, with blood sugar starting to rise above normal
items.4: Stage 3: type 1 diabetes is diagnosed
items.5: Two or more antibodies that last over time mean a high risk of type 1. Only 10 to 15% of people newly diagnosed have a family history
items.6: TrialNet screens relatives of people with type 1 at no cost, with a home finger-stick kit or a lab visit, anywhere in Canada. Immediate relatives aged 2 to 45 and other relatives aged 2 to 20 can take part. Results take 4 to 6 weeks
items.7: There is also FEDERATE-Can, in Quebec. CanScreen, a Canadian research program on screening newborns and children, says it is launching in fall 2026 or winter 2027
items.8: In Canada, the type 1 guidelines (2025) make no recommendation about screening
items.9: People who test positive are followed over time. International guidance says they should be taught, and reminded, about the signs of diabetes and DKA
items.10: In May 2025, Health Canada approved teplizumab (Tzield) for people aged 8 and older in stage 2, to delay stage 3. In one study it delayed stage 3 by about 2 years, and it can cause side effects, including serious ones. Canada’s Drug Agency recommended that public drug plans not cover it, and it isn’t on any provincial or territorial drug plan. It’s available out of pocket, through private insurance, or through compassionate access
items.11: You can ask your doctor to look at UncoverT1D, a website run by Sanofi, the company that makes teplizumab, that has information for health care providers about which tests to order

5.note: Whether to screen, and what a result means, is a conversation with your doctor. A screening result isn’t a diagnosis.

6.title: Could my type be different?

items.1: Your diabetes team decides your type. Some cases are difficult to classify
items.2: An international consensus found that more than 40% of people who develop type 1 after age 30 are first treated as type 2
items.3: The right type may change your treatment. International guidance adds that it can show whether your family might be offered testing

2.heading: Clues to mention to your team

items.1: You were diagnosed at a younger age, or you have a lower body weight
items.2: You lost weight without trying, or you’ve had ketones or DKA
items.3: You needed insulin within 1 to 2 years of diagnosis
items.4: Diabetes runs through generations of your family, such as a parent and a grandparent
items.5: You were diagnosed before 6 months of age
items.6: You have hearing loss, and there’s diabetes on your mother’s side of the family. International guidance links the two
items.7: You’ve had pancreas disease or surgery, or you have cystic fibrosis or iron overload (hemochromatosis)
items.8: Your diabetes started after a transplant, or after you began steroids, an antipsychotic, an anti-rejection medicine or cancer immunotherapy
items.9: You have a hormone condition, such as Cushing’s syndrome or acromegaly

items.1: Antibody tests look for signs of type 1. International guidance suggests testing for GAD antibodies first
items.2: A C-peptide test shows how much insulin your body still makes. It’s most useful months to years after diagnosis, and not during a very high blood sugar
items.3: Genetic tests look for single-gene types, such as MODY. A specialist usually arranges them
items.4: Antibody levels fade over time, and the tests aren’t accurate enough to use for everyone. When your type is hard to tell, a positive test points to type 1, but a negative test doesn’t rule type 1 out. Your team decides

items.1: Your doctor or specialist orders these tests. In Manitoba, for example, the GAD antibody test is ordered by endocrinologists, and other doctors need an approval form
items.2: What’s covered varies by province. In BC, for example, the antibody tests aren’t covered by MSP
items.3: Genetic testing usually needs a referral. A test that isn’t offered in your province may need approval before it’s sent elsewhere

6.note: Not a diagnostic tool. These clues are things to mention, not signs that your type is wrong. Your team decides what to test. Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist.

figure.printHeading: Questions to bring to your team

questions.1: Does my type still fit, given the clues I’ve ticked?
questions.2: Have I had antibody tests? What did they show?
questions.3: Would a C-peptide test help, and when?
questions.4: Should anyone in my family be tested?
questions.5: Would a specialist or a genetics clinic help?

figure.glossaryNote: Where Canadian guidance doesn’t explain a test, the meaning here comes from international guidance.

1.meaning: The antibody test most often done first when type 1 or LADA is possible.

2.meaning: Other type 1 antibodies, also used in screening. IA-2 and ZnT8 may be tested if the GAD test is negative.

3.meaning: Shows how much insulin your body still makes. It’s a blood or urine test.

4.meaning: A blood test that reflects your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months. It’s used to diagnose diabetes and prediabetes. With diabetes, it’s usually checked about every 3 months.

5.meaning: Your blood sugar is checked 2 hours after a 75 g glucose drink.

6.meaning: A genetic test that looks at many diabetes genes at once.

7.title: LADA: type 1 that starts slowly in adults

items.1: LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) is a slow-starting form of type 1. It’s sometimes called type 1.5
items.2: The usual pattern: it starts after age 30, antibodies are present, and insulin isn’t needed for at least the first 6 months
items.3: It’s often first diagnosed and managed as type 2
items.4: An antibody test, usually GAD, confirms it. International guidance says a C-peptide test helps guide treatment
items.5: Most people need insulin sooner than with type 2, and the timing varies widely. International guidance says it tends to come sooner with higher antibody levels, or more than one antibody
items.6: A modified type 1 plan can include some type 2 medicines. International guidance says others are less suitable, so ask your team before any change
items.7: Estimates of how common it is range from 2 to 12% of adult diabetes (international) to about 10% (Canadian)

7.note: Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist. Bring these questions to your team. The signs of lows and ketones are in Staying Safe.

figure.heading: LADA: questions to bring to your team

fields.1: Have I had an antibody test? What did it show?
fields.3: When should I check for ketones, and how?

8.title: MODY: single-gene diabetes

items.1: MODY is caused by a change in a single gene. In Canada, single-gene diabetes is called rare. International estimates range from 1 to 2% of diabetes for MODY to 1 to 5% for all single-gene types
items.2: International estimates suggest about 9 in 10 people with MODY are first told they have another type
items.3: Clues include being diagnosed young, not having obesity, having no type 1 antibodies, and a parent with diabetes, in two or more generations
items.4: How young varies. Canadian guidance, and some international guidance, use under 25. Other international guidance uses under 30, or 35 and under. Your team decides
items.5: It’s confirmed with a genetic test, usually after antibody and C-peptide tests
items.6: GCK: a mild, steady high blood sugar that usually needs no treatment
items.7: HNF1A and HNF4A: often treated with tablets rather than insulin. A specialist decides
items.8: HNF1B: can affect the kidneys, with cysts, and other organs. It’s usually treated with insulin
items.9: Each child of a parent with MODY has a 50% chance of inheriting it. Once the family’s gene change is known, relatives can be tested, and genetic counselling can help
items.10: In pregnancy with GCK, care depends on whether the baby inherited it, so tell your team early. HNF4A can mean a larger baby, and low blood sugar in the newborn
items.11: In a Canadian study of children with single-gene diabetes, GCK was the most common type: 19 of 29 children
items.12: Most of the evidence comes from people of European ancestry. The usual clues are less reliable for people of other ancestries

8.note: Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist. Fill in the family tree before your appointment. It helps your team, or a genetic counsellor, see the pattern.

familyTree.heading: My family diabetes tree
familyTree.intro: For your appointment. Fill in what you know and leave the rest blank. It doesn’t work out a risk, and nothing you type is saved or sent.

sides.yours: Me, my brothers and sisters, and my children

9.title: Diabetes in babies

items.1: Diabetes diagnosed before 6 months of age is usually caused by a single gene
items.2: Every baby diagnosed before 6 months should have genetic testing
items.3: International estimates are about 1 in 100,000 births and about 1 in 90,000. It is described as occurring in the first 6 to 12 months
items.4: Some forms are temporary, and others are lifelong
items.5: The genetic result matters. For the potassium-channel types, international guidance says about 9 in 10 people can switch from insulin to tablets under specialist care, with more benefit the earlier it happens
items.6: Adults told they have type 1 who were diagnosed before 6 months should have their diagnosis reviewed

9.note: Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change in treatment is planned with a specialist team.

10.title: Genetic syndromes with diabetes

items.1: Some single-gene types come with other health signs, such as hearing loss or vision loss
items.2: MIDD (maternally inherited diabetes and deafness) passes from a mother to all her children, though how much it affects each child varies. Fathers don’t pass it on
items.3: Diabetes starts at 37 on average, and insulin is usually needed within about 2 years
items.4: Hearing loss is common and often comes first. The heart, kidneys, eyes and gut can be affected too
items.5: A urine sample is preferred for the test
items.6: Wolfram syndrome is very rare, about 1 in 500,000 people, and both parents carry the gene. Diabetes usually starts around age 6, and vision loss from the optic nerve around age 11
items.7: Lipodystrophy affects where the body stores fat. Clues include little or unusually placed body fat, high triglycerides (a blood fat), and darkened skin in body folds
items.8: These are confirmed with genetic testing, arranged through a specialist

10.note: If several of these sound familiar, ask your team whether a genetics referral would help.

11.title: Pancreas conditions and iron overload

items.1: Diseases of the pancreas can cause diabetes, including pancreatitis, surgery or injury to the pancreas, a growth in the pancreas, and cystic fibrosis
items.2: Hemochromatosis, where the body stores too much iron, is another cause. It can affect the pancreas and lead to diabetes
items.3: About 1 in 300 Canadians have two copies of the gene change that puts them at risk. Fewer than 1 in 10 of them develop the disease
items.4: An iron test isn’t part of a standard blood test, so it has to be asked for. A genetic test confirms hemochromatosis
items.5: Close family, such as parents, brothers, sisters and children, should be tested
items.6: Treatment removes blood regularly (phlebotomy). It can mildly improve diabetes

11.note: If you’ve had pancreas disease or surgery, ask your team what it means for your diabetes care. Lows and ketones are covered in Staying Safe.

12.title: Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes

items.1: Cystic fibrosis can affect the pancreas and lead to diabetes, called cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD)
items.2: It becomes more common with age. In Canada, 3.6% of people with CF under 18 have it, rising to 58.7% of adults over 35
items.3: Screening is yearly from age 10, through your CF clinic. Canadian guidelines start with an A1C test and add a glucose tolerance test when needed. The glucose tolerance test may be used first if A1C isn’t reliable for you. Your clinic decides
items.4: Insulin is the main treatment, and the only medicine used for children. Some adults may have other options
items.5: If you use insulin, ask your team for a plan for lows. Canadian guidelines say people on insulin, and their families or carers, should be taught how to use glucagon. International guidance adds that the body’s own response to a low is weaker in CF
items.6: In pregnancy, if you don’t already have CFRD, a glucose tolerance test is done early, at 12 to 16 weeks or when the pregnancy is confirmed. If that one is normal, it’s repeated at 24 to 28 weeks
items.7: After a transplant, 25 to 50% of people with CF who didn’t have CFRD before develop diabetes
items.8: Yearly eye, kidney and nerve checks start 5 years after diagnosis
items.9: Your CF clinic works with a diabetes team, ideally including a diabetes educator

12.note: Glucagon and <link>the Rule of 15</link> are in Staying Safe.

13.title: From medicines, or after a transplant

items.1: Some medicines can cause diabetes, including steroids, some antipsychotics and some anti-rejection medicines
items.2: In hospital, 20 to 50% of people without diabetes who take steroids develop high blood sugar. Checking blood sugar for 48 hours after starting may be considered
items.3: Some antipsychotic medicines can cause weight gain and raise blood sugar and cholesterol
items.4: In children and teens, the risk of type 2 diabetes is 2 to 3 times higher, and the rise can show within the first year
items.5: Canadian guidelines recommend checking weight, blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol before you start, then on a schedule that differs for each check. Ask your prescriber when yours are due
items.6: International guidance says to check blood sugar before you start a checkpoint inhibitor, a type of cancer immunotherapy, and at every visit while you’re on it. An international consensus says this diabetes can come on with DKA
items.7: After a transplant, the risk depends on things like the steroid dose, some infections, and which anti-rejection medicine is used
items.8: Canadian guidelines call for checking blood sugar before the transplant, in the first 3 months after it, and with an A1C at 3 and 12 months, then every year. A glucose tolerance test is more sensitive than A1C, and it’s used if A1C isn’t reliable. Your team decides
items.9: An international consensus says 20 to 40% of people who have a heart, lung or liver transplant develop diabetes
items.10: Know the <link>signs of high blood sugar and ketones</link>. They’re in Staying Safe

13.note: Don’t stop or change how you take any of these medicines on your own, even if your blood sugar goes up. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist first.

1.heading: Your doctor or specialist
1.body: Orders antibody, C-peptide and A1C tests. Some labs limit antibody tests to specialists unless an approval form is sent. Bring your clues: see Could my type be different?

2.heading: A genetics clinic
2.body: Single-gene testing usually needs a referral. A test not offered in your province may need approval first. See MODY: single-gene diabetes.

3.heading: TrialNet, for relatives
3.body: Free type 1 antibody screening for relatives, at home or at a lab, anywhere in Canada. See Type 1 starts before symptoms.

4.heading: Your CF clinic
4.body: Yearly diabetes screening from age 10 for people with cystic fibrosis. See Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes.

pharmacist.heading: Questions about pumps, sensors, supplies or claims
pharmacist.body: Liivv’s Certified Diabetes Educators answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to Liivv’s pharmacy in your province. Questions about your type, and the tests for it, belong with your diabetes team.

closing.heading: Knowing your type
closing.body: Your type shapes your care, and it can be looked at again if something doesn’t fit. Bring your clues and your questions to your team.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a diagnosis. Your diabetes team decides your type, which tests you need, and your treatment.

this-might-be-you.title: This Might Be You
this-might-be-you.heroBody: Pregnancy with type 1 or 2, a child with type 1, school and later life, and the people who help: what changes, and who to ask.
this-might-be-you.focus: Seasons of life: pregnancy with type 1 or type 2, a child with type 1, school, and later life. Care and community: caring for someone with diabetes, and NIHB coverage for First Nations and Inuit.
this-might-be-you.vibe: Specific and quick to refer: short on advice, clear on who to ask.

categoriesIntro.heading: When the usual advice isn’t enough
categoriesIntro.body: Most diabetes information is written for an adult managing on their own. These are the times when the details change, and the best next step is usually a conversation with a particular person.

startHere.heading: A season of life, or someone you care for?

1.title: Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2

items.1: Canadian guidelines recommend planning a pregnancy with your diabetes team before you start trying
items.2: Their A1C target before conception is 7.0% or lower, and 6.5% or lower if it can be done safely. Your team sets yours
items.3: They recommend starting folic acid before you conceive. With diabetes, you may need a higher dose than is usually advised, so ask your team or pharmacist how much to take
items.4: Bring a list of all your medicines, so your team can review them before you try. Some medicines need to be stopped or changed before pregnancy. Don’t stop any on your own
items.5: They also recommend an eye exam and a kidney check before you conceive

items.1: Blood sugar targets are tighter in pregnancy. Your team will give you yours
items.2: With type 1, Canadian guidelines recommend a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) in pregnancy. With type 2, ask your team whether one suits you
items.3: They also recommend another eye exam in the first trimester
items.4: In pregnancy, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) can happen even when blood sugar is normal or only a little high. DKA needs medical care right away

items.1: If you use insulin, your needs drop quickly after the birth. Plan the change with your team before you deliver. Lows are more likely in the first days, so check more often
items.2: Canadian guidelines encourage breastfeeding
items.3: They also recommend an eye exam within the first year after the birth

1.note: Gestational diabetes, which starts in pregnancy, is in <link>Know Your Type</link>. The pregnancy guidance this card draws on is from 2018 and is being updated.

fields.2: Folic acid: how much, and when to start
fields.3: My medicines: what stays the same, and what changes
fields.4: Eye and kidney checks booked for
fields.5: Who to call while I’m pregnant

2.title: A child with type 1

items.1: For type 1, Canadian guidelines set the same A1C target for children of every age: below 7.0%. Your child’s team sets theirs
items.2: Younger children take less fast-acting sugar for a low, depending on their age. The amounts are in <link>The Rule of 15</link>
items.3: From age 4, glucagon can be a nasal spray or an injection. For a child under 4, ask your child’s team which glucagon to keep
items.4: Check for ketones when your child is sick or their blood sugar stays high. The ranges are in <link>Ketones: check and act</link>
items.5: Canadian guidelines say regular check-ins on emotional health are especially helpful in the teen years and young adulthood
items.6: Type 1 diabetes meets the Disability Tax Credit’s life-sustaining therapy test for 2021 and later tax years. You still apply with form T2201, on paper or online, and your child’s doctor or nurse practitioner fills in their part
items.7: Once a child is approved for the credit, a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) can be opened for them
items.8: Some provincial pump programs have separate rules for children. In Quebec, a child has to join the pump program before age 18
items.9: Kidney checks usually start 5 years after diagnosis, or after puberty if your child was diagnosed young. Eye exams usually start at age 15, once your child has had type 1 for 5 years. Your child’s team sets the schedule

2.note: Your child’s diabetes clinic is the first call for anything about their plan. Programs by province are in <link>Funding & Coverage</link>.

3.title: Your child at school

items.1: A student’s care plan has two parts: a daily diabetes management plan and a diabetes emergency plan
items.2: The principal should work with you, your child and your child’s health care team to write the plan
items.3: Talk it through with the school before the school year starts, and ask for at least two staff to be trained
items.4: Students should be able to check their blood sugar, take insulin, and treat lows and highs wherever and whenever they need to
items.5: Schools should let students carry a phone or smartwatch to help manage their blood sugar
items.6: Lows at school are common for students with type 1. They’re no cause for alarm, but they need treating right away, where they happen
items.7: Don’t leave a student alone if a low is suspected. If they’re unresponsive, have a seizure or can’t take sugar by mouth, it’s an emergency: have someone call 911, turn them on their side, stay with them, and put nothing in their mouth
items.8: Then, if the care plan includes consent for glucagon, staff named in the plan, and trained, give it
items.9: For type 1, Canadian guidelines call for help with giving insulin at school and daycare across Canada

3.note: School rules differ by province and territory, and Diabetes Canada compares them. Diabetes@School, from the Canadian Paediatric Society and its partners, has more for families and school staff.

fields.1: Who at school is trained (at least two people)
fields.2: Where the low supplies are kept
fields.3: Glucagon: is it in the plan, and who gives it
fields.4: How my child checks their blood sugar at school
fields.5: Who the school calls first, and the backup number
fields.6: Who calls 911 for a severe low

4.title: Later life

items.1: Canadian guidelines for older people set targets by how healthy and independent someone is
items.2: For people who are healthy and independent, the A1C target is 7.0% or lower
items.3: For people who take medicine that can cause lows, Canadian guidelines say a less strict A1C target may be considered: 7.1 to 8.0% for people who are functionally dependent, and 7.1 to 8.5% for people who are frail or living with dementia. Your team sets yours. Near the end of life, A1C tests are no longer recommended. The aim then is to avoid any lows, and highs that cause symptoms
items.4: Canadian guidelines put a strong focus on preventing lows in older people
items.5: If injecting is getting harder, ask your team about simpler options. Prefilled insulin pens are one way to cut down on dose mistakes
items.6: Changes in memory or thinking can make a new skill, like injecting, harder to learn. Tell your team, so they can plan around it
items.7: In Ontario, people 65 and older who use insulin every day and live at home can apply to the Assistive Devices Program for $170 a year toward syringes and needles

4.note: Ask a pharmacist to go through your full list of medicines, including anything you buy without a prescription. More programs for seniors are in <link>Funding & Coverage</link>.

5.title: Caring for someone with diabetes

items.1: The most useful things to learn are what a low and a high look like, <link>the Rule of 15</link>, and when to call for help. They’re all in Staying Safe
items.2: If they have glucagon, ask to be shown how it works. Canadian guidelines say the people around them should be taught
items.3: Ask what kind of help is wanted before you offer it
items.4: Breakthrough T1D has a caregiver guide for parents and caregivers of children and teens with type 1
items.5: Its Mental Health + Diabetes Directory lists registered mental health providers, for people living with diabetes and the people affected by it
items.6: Low mood and worry about lows are common with diabetes, and Canadian guidelines ask teams to check for them

5.note: If caring is wearing you down, tell your own doctor. Canadian guidelines say parents and caregivers of young people with diabetes should be checked for diabetes distress too.

figure.body: If you’re thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time of day or night. If your safety is at risk right now, call 911.

6.title: First Nations and Inuit: NIHB coverage

items.1: Indigenous Services Canada runs the federal Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program for First Nations and Inuit
items.2: Who is eligible is set out on <link>Indigenous Services Canada’s eligibility page</link>. Liivv can’t decide whether you’re eligible. For questions about eligibility, Indigenous Services Canada says to contact your NIHB regional office
items.3: For people who manage diabetes with insulin, NIHB covers several continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), with prior approval. The list is in <link>the NIHB program updates</link>
items.4: It also covers up to 800 test strips every 100 days for people who use insulin
items.5: If you aren’t covered by NIHB, <link>Funding & Coverage</link> lists the programs in each province and territory

6.note: NIHB adds items to its list from time to time. Your pharmacist can check what’s covered today.

1.heading: Planning a pregnancy
1.body: Your diabetes team, before you start trying, to go over your A1C, your medicines, and your eyes and kidneys. More in Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2.

2.heading: A child starting school
2.body: The principal, with you, your child and their diabetes team, before the school year starts. More in Your child at school.

3.heading: Later life
3.body: Your diabetes team, for targets that fit your health, and a pharmacist, for your full list of medicines. More in Later life.

4.heading: Someone you care for
4.body: Staying Safe for the basics, and Breakthrough T1D’s caregiver guide if it’s a child or teen with type 1. More in Caring for someone with diabetes.

pharmacist.heading: Supply questions, whoever you’re shopping for
pharmacist.body: Liivv’s Certified Diabetes Educators answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to Liivv’s pharmacy in your province. Questions about a pregnancy, a child’s plan or a change in someone’s health belong with their diabetes team.

closing.heading: The same diabetes, a different season
closing.body: What changes is who to bring in, and when. Knowing that is most of the work.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice. Care in pregnancy, for children and in later life differs in ways this page doesn’t try to cover. It tells you what changes and who to ask. Your diabetes team sets your targets and your plan.

urgentExit.lead: Signs that need emergency care are in Staying Safe, under

type.other: Another type (such as LADA or type 3c), or not sure

therapy.nonInsulin: Tablets, or injections that aren’t insulin

fed-nihb.covered: NIHB continues to cover these glucose sensors (CGM) for clients who manage their diabetes with insulin: FreeStyle Libre 2, Dexcom G6 and G7, and Guardian Connect. FreeStyle Libre 3 with prior approval, at one reader every 3 years and 14 sensors every 6 months. Guardian 4, as a limited use benefit with prior approval, for people with type 1 aged 19 or under on intensive insulin who use a MiniMed 780G. If you use insulin, test strips up to 800 every 100 days.
fed-nihb.who: Who is eligible is set out on Indigenous Services Canada’s NIHB pages. Liivv can’t decide whether you’re eligible: ask NIHB or your pharmacy.
fed-nihb.howToApply: NIHB covers items on its Drug Benefit List when they aren’t covered by provincial or territorial health insurance, private insurance or another public plan. Pharmacies enrolled with NIHB generally bill it directly, so you don’t pay a deductible or co-payment: you show your client identification. Some items, such as some sensors, need prior approval first.

fed-vac.covered: A continuous glucose monitor for type 1 diabetes, under benefit code 401140, once every 5 calendar years, with a prescription from a doctor or nurse practitioner. A replacement device doesn’t need a new prescription.
fed-vac.who: If you’re a Veterans Affairs Canada client with type 1 diabetes, this benefit may cover you. Ask Veterans Affairs Canada whether it applies to you.
fed-vac.howToApply: It needs pre-authorization, so get that before you buy.
fed-vac.notes: Veterans Affairs Canada’s general medical supplies policy also names diabetic test strips, syringes and needles among its examples.

on-adp-pump.covered: 100% of the ADP price of an insulin pump. For pump supplies, up to $2,400 a year, paid to you as $600 every 3 months.
on-adp-pump.who: People with type 1 diabetes who meet the program’s medical criteria. It isn’t based on income. If WSIB or Veterans Affairs Canada already pays for the same items, ADP doesn’t.
on-adp-pump.howToApply: An ADP-registered diabetes education program assesses you, and an ADP-registered vendor sends in the application. ADP aims to review applications within 8 weeks, and the first $600 is sent within 30 days of approval. Renew pump supplies every year.
on-adp-pump.notes: After the 5-year warranty, a worn-out pump can be replaced; ADP asks for a repair quote. A replacement is also covered if your medical needs have changed. ADP doesn’t cover replacing a lost pump or supplies, or repairing ones damaged through misuse or neglect.

bc-pharmacare-pumps.covered: One insulin pump every 5 years: the Omnipod 5 or Omnipod DASH system, the mylife YpsoPump, or the MiniMed 670G, 770G or 780G. On Fair PharmaCare you pay until you reach your deductible, then PharmaCare pays 70%, and 100% once you reach your family maximum. On Plans B, C, F and W it pays 100%. Pump supplies (pods, infusion sets, reservoirs and cartridges) are covered whether or not PharmaCare paid for your pump, with no Special Authority needed; batteries and adhesive pads aren’t.
bc-pharmacare-pumps.who: People covered by Fair PharmaCare or Plan B, C, F or W, with type 1 or another form of diabetes that needs insulin, whose endocrinologist or diabetes specialist confirms they meet the medical criteria.
bc-pharmacare-pumps.howToApply: Your specialist sends PharmaCare a Special Authority request. If it’s approved, you get a copy of the approval letter to take to the pump maker; the approval lasts 6 months. Wait for the letter before you buy: PharmaCare can’t cover a pump bought before approval. Pump supplies are covered when a pharmacy or an approved pump vendor submits the claim on PharmaNet; PharmaCare doesn’t take paper claims for them.
bc-pharmacare-pumps.notes: No Tandem pump is on PharmaCare’s list of covered pumps. Tandem pump supplies, such as t:slim cartridges and AutoSoft, TruSteel and VariSoft infusion sets, are on its list of diabetes products.

ab-iptp.covered: An insulin pump every 5 years from an approved maker (Medtronic, Ypsomed, Insulet or Tandem), its supplies, and other diabetes management supplies, up to set limits.
ab-iptp.who: Alberta residents enrolled in, or eligible for, the Alberta Health Care Insurance Plan, with type 1 or type 3c diabetes, who meet the program’s clinical criteria. Adults have a review every year, and children under 18 every 6 months.
ab-iptp.howToApply: Through an approved insulin pump clinic: you attend a pre-pump information session, complete an education plan, have at least one assessment and sign a Patient Responsibility Form. The clinic then sends Alberta Blue Cross an eligibility form, and Alberta Blue Cross mails you a confirmation letter. Pumps come straight from an approved maker, and supplies from a licensed Alberta pharmacy or an approved maker, which bill the program directly. The program doesn’t pay you back for a pump or supplies you pay for yourself.
ab-iptp.notes: Since October 1, 2026, Alberta’s government programs, this one included, pay only after any private or workplace plan you have.

sk-pump.covered: A $6,300 grant toward one insulin pump every 5 years. Pump supplies follow your Drug Plan coverage, so deductibles and co-payments apply.
sk-pump.who: People with type 1 diabetes who would benefit from a pump and meet the program’s criteria.
sk-pump.howToApply: A Saskatchewan Health Authority diabetes education program, or an authorized diabetes specialist physician, sends in the application. For children, it goes through the Saskatchewan Health Authority’s pediatric diabetes education program, after an information session or an online module.

mb-pump.covered: One approved insulin pump every 5 years, ordered from an approved supplier at no cost to you, with no deductible. Pump supplies aren’t part of it: they can be covered by Manitoba Pharmacare, where your deductible applies.
mb-pump.who: Manitobans 18 and over with type 1 diabetes whom an endocrinologist, or the doctor who manages their diabetes, recommends for a pump. You can’t have had a pump from a Manitoba government program in the last 5 years, or have coverage under a federal program.
mb-pump.howToApply: Your endocrinologist or doctor sends the application to Manitoba Health for you. If it’s approved, you get a letter telling you how to order your pump directly from the supplier.
mb-pump.notes: Children have a separate program, the Manitoba Pediatric Insulin Pump Program (MPIPP). Ask your child’s diabetes team about it.

qc-pump.covered: Up to $6,300 toward a pump every 5 years, and up to $4,000 a year for pump supplies.
qc-pump.who: You have to join before you turn 18. You can stay in after 18, with a review each year. Adults diagnosed later can’t join.
qc-pump.howToApply: For supplies, send your original receipts or insurance statements to the program’s paying agent, the CHU de Québec – Université Laval. With some companies you don’t pay for supplies at all, because the CHU refunds the company directly.
qc-pump.notes: The program’s page was last updated on February 19, 2021, so check the current amounts with the program.

nb-ipp.covered: Insulin pumps, pump supplies and glucose sensors (CGM), for the part that isn’t covered by other insurance.
nb-ipp.who: Pumps: type 1, at any age. Sensors: type 1, or type 2 with 3 or more insulin injections a day. It’s based on income, and private insurance has to be used first. If your insurance already covers 100% of the cost, you can’t join.
nb-ipp.howToApply: For pumps, an endocrinologist, internist or pediatrician confirms you meet the medical criteria; for sensors, the health care provider who manages your diabetes does. If you apply for both, the same specialist confirms both. Then you apply online. Devices and supplies come only from the program’s approved vendors, not from pharmacies. You pay your share to the vendor, and the vendor bills the province for the rest.
nb-ipp.notes: Insulin, test strips and batteries aren’t covered by this program.

ns-ipp.covered: One insulin pump every 5 years (Tandem, Medtronic or Insulet), plus pump supplies. You pay a yearly share based on your income and family size, with no premiums or deductibles.
ns-ipp.who: People with type 1 diabetes, diagnosed at least 4 months ago.
ns-ipp.howToApply: Contact the Insulin Pump Program to confirm you’re eligible. It connects you with an approved Diabetes Health Centre, which completes and sends a Clinical Eligibility Form for you. Then fill in the funding application (one form for adults, one for children and youth) and mail it with your supporting documents. A decision takes about 1 to 2 weeks. Renew between January 1 and March 31 every year.
ns-ipp.notes: Glucose sensors aren’t part of this program. Nova Scotia has a separate Sensor-based Glucose Monitoring Program, shown under sensor programs.

pe-ipp.covered: Up to 100% of the cost of a pump and its supplies, shipped every 3 months, depending on your household income, any private insurance and the device’s cost. Approved pumps: Medtronic, Omnipod and Tandem. Glucose sensors aren’t part of it: PEI has a separate Glucose Sensor Program.
pe-ipp.who: PEI residents of any age with type 1 diabetes whom the Provincial Diabetes Program finds medically eligible.
pe-ipp.howToApply: Your family doctor or nurse practitioner can refer you to the Provincial Diabetes Program, whose team decides whether you’re medically eligible. You then complete the program’s application with your pump team. You pay your share straight to the pump company, usually every 3 months before your supplies ship. Renew every year between April 1 and June 30.
pe-ipp.notes: If you have private insurance, its share is taken off before the program works out its own, so ask your insurer for written confirmation of your coverage. What you pay for the pump or its supplies doesn’t count toward the Catastrophic Drug Program’s household cap.

nl-pump.covered: Basic insulin pumps and supplies, for people with type 1 diabetes who qualify. Since January 18, 2021, new clients 18 and over have an income test to work out whether they pay part of the cost, with a financial hardship policy.
nl-pump.who: People with type 1 diabetes who qualify medically. Children and youth up to 18 have full coverage.
nl-pump.notes: These details come from a 2021 government news release. Eastern Health ran the program then, and its pages have since moved, so check the current details with your diabetes team.

yt-pump.covered: Yukon’s National Pharmacare Program gives access to newer insulin pump technology, such as the Omnipod 5 system. Pump eligibility is granted every 5 years.
yt-pump.notes: The program’s page doesn’t say how much of a pump is covered or how to apply. For questions about diabetes equipment or supplies, it points you to Chronic Disease and Disability Benefits or the Senior Pharmacare Program.

on-adp-cgm.covered: Full coverage of real-time CGM sensors and transmitters, and in some cases a receiver, up to a set quantity every 2 years.
on-adp-cgm.who: People with type 1 diabetes who meet the program’s criteria.
on-adp-cgm.howToApply: Your diabetes education program can tell you whether you meet the criteria. Coverage is renewed every 2 years.

on-odb-cgm.covered: Dexcom G7 since July 31, 2025, up to 45 sensors a year, and FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus since November 28, 2025, up to 31 sensors a year, with a receiver or reader.
on-odb-cgm.who: People covered by the Ontario Drug Benefit who take insulin for diabetes. That includes people 65 and over, and people 24 and under with no private plan (OHIP+).
on-odb-cgm.howToApply: You need a prescription from a doctor or nurse practitioner. The pharmacy claims it from the Ontario Drug Benefit.

bc-cgm.covered: Dexcom G6 and G7, FreeStyle Libre 2 and FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus are on PharmaCare’s list of diabetes devices. All of them need Special Authority before PharmaCare will cover them.
bc-cgm.howToApply: Ask your diabetes team or pharmacist about Special Authority before you order.

ab-cgm.covered: Dexcom G6 and G7, FreeStyle Libre 2 and 3 Plus, and Medtronic sensors, up to yearly limits, such as 37 Dexcom G7 sensors or 25 FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus sensors. Co-payments apply, and sensors don’t count toward the yearly limit on diabetes supplies.
ab-cgm.who: Albertans enrolled in one of Alberta’s government-sponsored health benefit plans. Under 18: any ongoing insulin or insulin pump therapy. 18 and over: an insulin pump, a basal-bolus insulin or a premixed insulin.
ab-cgm.howToApply: Get your sensors at a pharmacy. For adults, Medtronic sensors need Special Authorization first.
ab-cgm.notes: Since October 1, 2026, these plans pay only after any private or workplace plan you have.

mb-cgm.covered: Continuous and flash glucose monitors, through regular Pharmacare. Your Pharmacare deductible applies.
mb-cgm.who: Type 1 or type 2 diabetes managed with several insulin injections a day (basal-bolus) or an insulin pump.
mb-cgm.howToApply: You don’t need a special application.

qc-cgm.covered: FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus (listed since December 11, 2025) and Dexcom G6 and G7 are on Quebec’s public plan list as exception drugs. Since February 4, 2026, the same criteria apply to every continuous glucose monitor on the list.
qc-cgm.who: People 2 and over. Under 18: type 1 diabetes. 18 and over: intensive insulin therapy (an insulin pump, or at least 3 injections a day of at least 2 different insulins), plus at least one of these: an A1C that stays above your target despite optimal care, frequent lows in the past year, or not being able to recognize or report the signs of a low.
qc-cgm.howToApply: Your prescriber asks for coverage as an exception. The first approval lasts 6 months. It’s renewed if you wear the sensor at least 70% of the time.
qc-cgm.notes: Quebec’s public plan generally doesn’t cover prescription drugs bought outside Quebec. Check the details with RAMQ.

ns-sbgm.covered: Approved sensors and supplies listed in the Nova Scotia Formulary, dispensed by a pharmacy with a prescription. There’s a yearly deductible based on family income: $0 up to $60,000, $500 up to $80,000, $750 up to $100,000 and $1,000 up to $150,000. There are no premiums or co-payments.
ns-sbgm.who: Nova Scotia residents aged 2 and over with a valid Health Card and a household income of $150,000 or less, with type 1 or type 2 diabetes on intensive insulin therapy (at least 4 injections a day) or an insulin pump.
ns-sbgm.howToApply: Fill in the registration form (a doctor, nurse practitioner or pharmacist completes its last page) and submit it online or by mail. Enrolment takes 1 to 2 weeks and renews automatically each February. You pay the full cost at the pharmacy until you reach your deductible.
ns-sbgm.notes: Private insurance has to be used first. The program doesn’t cover prescriptions bought outside Nova Scotia except in very specific cases.

nl-cgm.covered: Full or partial coverage of glucose sensors (CGM).
nl-cgm.who: In May 2025, the province announced that from fall 2025 the program would be open to everyone with type 1 diabetes who meets its medical and income criteria.
nl-cgm.notes: The program started in 2023 for children with type 1. In 2024 it grew to include young people up to age 24, and pregnancy and gestational diabetes. Ask the program what it covers for you now.

on-odb-strips.covered: Test strips each year: 3,000 if you use insulin; 400 if you take a diabetes medicine with a higher risk of lows; 200 with a lower-risk medicine; 200 if you manage with diet and lifestyle alone. More needs a reason from your doctor or nurse practitioner.
on-odb-strips.who: People covered by the Ontario Drug Benefit. That includes people 65 and over, and people 24 and under with no private plan (OHIP+).

on-mfhp.covered: 75% of the cost of a blood glucose meter, up to $75 once every 5 years, and 75% of the cost of test strips and lancets, up to $920 a year. For a talking meter, if a letter from your doctor confirms visual impairment, up to $300 once every 5 years.
on-mfhp.who: People who use insulin (type 1 or type 2), and people with gestational diabetes, who have no other coverage for these supplies. If you’re 65 or over, on social assistance or a Trillium Drug Program client, you can claim only for lancets and a blood glucose meter.
on-mfhp.howToApply: Diabetes Canada runs this program for Ontario. Your first claim form has to be signed by a doctor or nurse practitioner. Mail in the claim form with your original receipts. Processing takes about 8 weeks.

on-adp-seniors.covered: $170 a year toward insulin syringes and needles.
on-adp-seniors.who: People 65 and over who need insulin every day and live at home.
on-adp-seniors.howToApply: Buy them from any retailer in Ontario that sells them. Renew every 2 years. ADP pays you by direct deposit or cheque.

bc-np-supplies.covered: Since April 1, 2026, up to 400 lancets, 300 alcohol swabs and 100 blood or urine ketone strips a year, through Fair PharmaCare and Plans C, F and W (100% on Plans C, F and W). Coverage is processed at the pharmacy counter.
bc-np-supplies.who: You need training from a diabetes education centre or primary care network first. If you’re not on Plan C, F or W, register for Fair PharmaCare.

nl-strips.covered: Test strips a year: 2,500 with short-acting insulin; 700 with long-acting insulin only, plus 100 more with Special Authorization; 100 with non-insulin diabetes medicines only, plus 50; 50 with no diabetes medicine, plus 50 (fills 6 months apart). In pregnancy with gestational or type 2 diabetes, the quantity your health professional asks for.
nl-strips.who: People covered by the Newfoundland and Labrador Prescription Drug Program. A strip claim is paid only if a claim for a diabetes medicine was paid for you in the past year, or you have Special Authorization.
nl-strips.notes: The program pays last: if you have private insurance, the claim goes there first.

yt-cddb.covered: Diabetes is one of the program’s listed conditions. It can help with supplies such as syringes and glucose test kits, and equipment such as glucometers, when your health practitioner recommends them.
yt-cddb.howToApply: Your doctor applies to the program for you, before you buy. If you buy outside Yukon, you need the program’s approval first, or you pay and claim it back within 1 year.
yt-cddb.notes: It pays last: claim from any workplace or private plan first. There’s a yearly deductible.

nt-ehb.covered: Extended Health Benefits cover prescribed medical supplies and equipment on the NIHB Medical Supplies and Equipment list. Above income band 10, EHB pays 75% until your family reaches its maximum of $500 to $1,500. Income bands 2 to 10 pay nothing for now, and seniors 60 and over pay nothing.
nt-ehb.notes: We haven’t confirmed on an official page how EHB covers diabetes devices, so ask the program. EHB pays last. First Nations and Inuit residents use NIHB, and Métis residents the Métis Health Benefits Program.

mb-mepp.covered: Since April 15, 2025, most diabetes medicines at no cost and with no deductible. Ozempic isn’t included.
mb-mepp.howToApply: Bring your prescription and your Manitoba Health card to any Manitoba pharmacy.
mb-mepp.notes: Pumps, glucose sensors, test strips, syringes and lancets aren’t part of it. Glucose sensors and supplies are covered under regular Pharmacare, where your deductible applies. Adult insulin pumps are covered at no cost by a separate program, shown under pump programs.

bc-plan-np.covered: Since March 1, 2026, insulin and a set list of other diabetes medicines at no cost. A few others need Special Authority. Wider coverage of devices and supplies began on April 1, 2026.
bc-plan-np.who: It’s automatic if you’re enrolled in MSP. The prescription must be dispensed in B.C.

pe-pharmacare.covered: Since May 1, 2025, many diabetes medicines at no cost at any community pharmacy in PEI. Test strips cost $11 per 100 if you’re enrolled in PEI Pharmacare’s Diabetes Drug Program; with insulin, 100 strips up to every 25 days. Insulin syringes and pen needles aren’t covered.
pe-pharmacare.who: PEI residents with a valid PEI Health Card. Members of a federal plan, such as NIHB or Veterans Affairs Canada, keep that plan.
pe-pharmacare.notes: Prescriptions filled at a pharmacy outside PEI aren’t covered.

yt-pharmacare.covered: Diabetes medicines listed in the Yukon Drug Formulary are free at Yukon pharmacies, and the program pays first, even if you have private insurance. If you choose a brand-name drug when a lower-cost one is available, you pay the difference. It doesn’t cover diabetes equipment, supplies or glucose monitors, or medicines such as Ozempic.
yt-pharmacare.who: Yukon residents with Yukon health care coverage who aren’t covered by a federal drug program, such as NIHB or Veterans Affairs Canada. Enrolment is automatic.
yt-pharmacare.notes: Medicines filled outside Yukon aren’t covered.

fed-pharmacare.covered: The Pharmacare Act became law on October 10, 2024. Each province and territory has to sign its own agreement before anything changes where you live.
fed-pharmacare.notes: The federal government also announced a Diabetes Device Fund for devices and supplies in February 2024. The announcement said its details would follow discussions with the provinces and territories. We haven’t found an official page that says how to use it.

fed-dtc.covered: A tax credit for people whose impairment meets the CRA’s test. For diabetes, the usual route is life-sustaining therapy.
fed-dtc.who: If you have type 1, the CRA treats you as meeting the life-sustaining therapy test, from 2021 on. Otherwise, the therapy has to be needed at least 2 times a week, for an average of at least 14 hours a week, and the need has to have lasted, or be expected to last, at least 12 months. Time your pump spends delivering insulin doesn’t count toward the 14 hours.
fed-dtc.howToApply: Apply online or by phone with the CRA’s digital form, or by mail with the paper form T2201. Both parts of the application have to go in the same way. Even with type 1, you still have to apply.

fed-rdsp.covered: A long-term savings plan, with government grants and bonds.
fed-rdsp.who: You have to be approved for the Disability Tax Credit first, live in Canada and have a Social Insurance Number. You can open a plan until December 31 of the year you turn 59. Grants and bonds are paid only until the year you turn 49.

fed-medical-expenses.covered: What no program pays for may be claimable as a medical expense on your tax return. The CRA’s list includes insulin, needles and syringes, insulin pens, an insulin pump with its disposable parts, and a device to measure blood sugar, each with a prescription.

privateFirst.AB: Since October 1, 2026, Alberta’s government-sponsored programs, the Insulin Pump Therapy Program included, pay only after any private or workplace plan, so your private plan pays first. Tell your pharmacist about all the coverage you have.
privateFirst.NB: New Brunswick’s Insulin Pump Program covers only the part other insurance doesn’t, so your private plan pays first.
privateFirst.NS: Nova Scotia’s Insulin Pump Program pays after any other coverage you have, so your private plan pays first.
privateFirst.PE: PEI’s Insulin Pump Program takes off what your private insurance covers before it works out its own share, so your private plan pays first. Ask your insurer for written confirmation of your coverage.

liivv.pharmacies: Liivv’s pharmacies serve all of Canada, Quebec and the territories included. Insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec.
liivv.askUsTitle: Can we bill your program for you?
liivv.askUsBody: Our pharmacy in your province bills your provincial drug plan directly for what it covers, except in Quebec. For other programs, it depends on how each one pays: where one pays you back, ask us for an invoice for your claim. Ask us before you order and we’ll tell you where things stand.
liivv.quebecBody: Liivv’s pharmacies serve Quebec, but insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec. Quebec’s public drug plan generally doesn’t cover prescription drugs bought outside Quebec, so orders shipped to Quebec are paid for privately. For pump supplies, the Insulin Pump Access Program takes receipts, as shown below: ask us for an invoice for your claim.
liivv.territoryBody: Liivv’s pharmacies serve the territories too. Our pharmacies are in the provinces, so you pay for your order yourself. Check with your program that it will take your receipt before you order, and ask us for an invoice for your claim.

type-1.title: Type 1
type-1.heroBody: Insulin every day, lows and ketones, sensors and pumps: the cards that matter most with type 1, in one order.

body.1: With type 1, your pancreas makes no insulin, so you take insulin by injection or with a pump. 5 to 10% of people with diabetes have type 1, and it can start in adulthood too. An estimated 71% of people with type 1 in Canada were diagnosed as adults.
body.2: This path puts the cards that matter most with type 1 in one order. They cover how to treat a low and when to check for ketones, the sensors, pens and pumps you may use, and the times in life when the details change. Canadian guidelines prefer automated insulin delivery for anyone with type 1 who is willing and able to use it, so the pump and sensor cards are here too. Your team decides your plan with you.

type-2.title: Type 2
type-2.heroBody: From the first numbers to the yearly checkups: the cards that matter most with type 2, in one order.

body.1: Type 2 is the most common type. 90 to 95% of people with diabetes in Canada have it, and it may cause no symptoms at all. Treatment is different for each person. Many people with type 2 need insulin to stay healthy. Whether you do, and when, is decided with your team.
body.2: This path starts with the basics. Next come checking your blood sugar at home and the times a low can happen, then the checkups that look after your feet, eyes, kidneys and heart. If your diabetes doesn’t fit the usual picture, read Could my type be different? LADA, a type 1 that starts slowly in adults, is often first treated as type 2.

gestational.title: Gestational diabetes
gestational.heroBody: During your pregnancy, and the test that comes after the birth: the cards that matter most with gestational diabetes, in one order.

body.1: Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar first found during pregnancy. It affects 3 to 20% of pregnancies and usually goes away after the birth. Screening for it is offered between 24 and 28 weeks, or earlier if you’re at higher risk. Many people manage it with healthy eating and activity. Some also need medicine, such as insulin.
body.2: It still matters after the birth. It raises the chance of type 2 later, for you and your child, and a glucose tolerance test is recommended between 6 weeks and 6 months after the birth. This path covers your pregnancy first, then the reminder for afterwards. If you had diabetes before you were pregnant, read Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2 instead.
