prediabetes.title: Prediabetes
prediabetes.heroBody: What your numbers mean, and the everyday cards on food and movement.

body.1: Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal, but not high enough to be called type 2 diabetes. Not everyone with prediabetes goes on to develop type 2, but many people do.
body.2: This path keeps to the everyday: what your numbers mean, and the cards on food and movement. If losing weight is right for you, healthy changes that lead to a loss of 5% of your starting weight can delay or prevent type 2. Regular activity also lowers your risk, and a registered dietitian can help you find changes that suit you. Ask your doctor what your numbers mean for you, and when to test again.

intro.heading: When your type is less common

body.1: Most people have type 1 or type 2, but some cases are difficult to classify, and there are other forms too. These include LADA, a type 1 that starts slowly in adults, and single-gene types such as MODY. Diabetes can also be linked to the pancreas, cystic fibrosis, iron overload or some medicines, and it can start after a transplant.
body.2: The right type matters, because it may change your treatment. This path starts with the clues worth raising with your team, then gives each less common type its own card. Cards that rest on international guidance say so. Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything here. Any change is made with your specialist.

faq.label: Frequently asked questions
faq.heading: Questions, answered with sources.
faq.note: Practical notes, not medical advice. Each answer lists where it comes from.

1.a: For a machine, yes. Use CPAP therapy only if you have a prescription from your doctor or nurse practitioner. Your prescription covers your equipment and your settings. Each machine must be set for the person using it. APAP and bilevel machines are more complex, and a sleep specialist should prescribe them. {machineLine} {rxMaskLine} Only trained professionals should change your machine’s settings, and Liivv never advises on them. In Ontario, it’s your right to choose your community respiratory therapy provider.
1.machineLine: Liivv doesn’t sell CPAP or other sleep apnea machines yet.
1.rxMaskLine: On Liivv, a complete mask, including a children’s mask, needs a CPAP prescription, which a Liivv pharmacist checks before your order ships. Parts and supplies, such as cushions, headgear, tubing and filters, go straight in your cart.

2.q: Can I take my CPAP on a plane?
2.a: Yes. A CPAP machine is allowed in your carry-on and in checked baggage. Bring it as carry-on when you fly. At security, you can either put it in a clear plastic bag you bring for screening, or leave the tubes and mask in the case and put only the main unit in a bin. The distilled water it uses is exempt from the liquid limits. You don’t need a document about your medical needs, but you can show one to the screening officer if you think it will help. For a packing list, go to <link>Travelling with CPAP</link>.

3.q: How often should I replace my mask and filter?
3.a: Follow the manual for your machine and mask first. General advice differs, so here it is side by side. Most machines are replaced every 3 to 5 years, and accessories every 3 to 12 months. Change the machine’s filter every 2 months, or as needed. Check your tubing and headgear, and replace them when they’re worn. Programs also set the most they cover. NIHB’s guidelines, for example, are up to 14 inlet filters a year, 2 a year for each type of mask with headgear (face, nasal or nasal pillow), and 2 a year for tubing. More may be considered case by case, with prior approval. If a plan pays for your equipment, check its replacement time frames before you order. For signs a part is worn, go to <link>Time to replace supplies</link>.

4.q: What if my machine or mask is recalled?
4.a: Each recall notice says what to do, so look up your model on the Government of Canada’s <link>recalls and safety alerts</link> site. For the 2021 recall of some Philips machines made before April 26, 2021, the advice was to talk to your doctor or medical device provider before you stop or change how you use your machine. Canadian specialist advice for people using these machines for sleep apnea was to contact their doctor soon and keep using the machine in the meantime. For those machines, the advice was also to stop ozone and UV cleaning, and to clean the machine only as the maker’s instructions say. Some masks have magnets that can affect some metal implants and devices, such as pacemakers, in you or in someone who lives with you, cares for you or shares your bed. For the masks in one 2022 advisory, the advice is to stop using the mask if anyone in that group has one of the listed implants. For other masks, check with the mask’s maker and your health care team. Read the warning in <link>Driving & Staying Safe</link>.

5.a: On Sleep Apnea Care pages, on CPAP product pages, and in a cart with CPAP supplies, we turn off advertising signals. What you read and buy there isn’t used for ads or to build ad audiences. The page address and title are left out of our site analytics, and so are the names of CPAP products.

is-it-sleep-apnea.title: Is It Sleep Apnea?
is-it-sleep-apnea.heroBody: Snoring, gasping, always tired? Here are the signs, how testing works in Canada, and what your results mean.
is-it-sleep-apnea.focus: The signs: what sleep apnea is, what others notice, how common it is, a checklist to take to your doctor, and two signposts, for trouble sleeping and for snoring. Getting tested: talking to your doctor, lab and home tests, reading your results, what happens next, and who to ask.
is-it-sleep-apnea.vibe: Clear and unhurried: what to notice, and what to ask.

categoriesIntro.heading: Only a sleep study can tell
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter helps you notice the signs and talk to your doctor about them. It can’t tell you whether you have sleep apnea. A sleep study does that.

1.title: What sleep apnea is

items.1: Sleep apnea means short pauses in your breathing while you sleep
items.2: A pause usually lasts 10 to 30 seconds. Then your brain wakes you just enough to take a breath. Most people don’t remember waking
items.3: Obstructive sleep apnea is the most common type. Your airway narrows or closes while you sleep, even though your body keeps trying to breathe
items.4: Central sleep apnea is less common. Your airway is open, but your brain doesn’t send the signal to breathe
items.5: Untreated, sleep apnea can lead to daytime sleepiness and trouble thinking clearly. It raises the risk of car crashes, high blood pressure, heart attack and stroke
items.6: Sleep apnea can be treated. Your Treatment Options covers the choices

1.note: Children can have sleep apnea too. In the day, it can show up as trouble concentrating, hyperactivity or irritability. See This Might Be You.

2.title: Signs others notice first

items.1: A bed partner or family member often notices the signs before you do
items.2: Many people with sleep apnea don’t know they snore or gasp at night
items.3: Loud snoring, most nights
items.4: Pauses in breathing, then a gasp or a choke
items.5: Restless sleep
items.6: What a bed partner has seen or heard helps your doctor. If you sleep alone, your doctor can still check for signs

2.note: If someone tells you they’ve noticed this, mention it to your doctor. The checklist below prints a list to take with you.

1.heading: What they may hear or see

3.title: How common it is

items.1: In 2016 and 2017, 6.4% of Canadians said a health professional had diagnosed them with sleep apnea
items.2: Among people aged 60 to 79, it was 12.8%, about three times as common as in younger adults
items.3: Men were twice as likely as women to report a diagnosis
items.4: Women’s signs are more often tiredness or trouble sleeping, and men’s more often snoring. So sleep apnea may be missed more often in women
items.5: Nearly a third of Canadian adults (30%) were at moderate or high risk, based on a short questionnaire and body measurements
items.6: Many people have sleep apnea without knowing it. In population studies, 86% to 95% of people with significant sleep apnea had never been diagnosed

3.note: If any of this sounds like you, the checklist below can help you talk to your doctor.

4.title: Signs to mention to your doctor

items.1: Signs vary from person to person. Being very sleepy during the day is the most common one
items.2: Women’s signs are more often tiredness or trouble sleeping. Men’s are more often snoring

items.1: Someone has heard you snore loudly, most nights
items.2: Someone has seen you stop breathing, gasp or choke in your sleep
items.3: You’re very sleepy during the day, and you don’t know why
items.4: You feel tired or worn out much of the time
items.5: You wake up with headaches
items.6: You wake up often in the night, or get up to pee
items.7: Your sleep doesn’t leave you feeling rested
items.8: You find it hard to concentrate or remember things
items.11: You’ve nodded off, or nearly, while driving

items.1: Anyone of any age can get sleep apnea
items.2: It’s more likely if you’re male or over 40
items.3: It’s more likely if it runs in your family
items.4: It’s more likely with a large, thick neck or a lot of extra weight, or with large tonsils or a recessed chin

4.note: Not a diagnostic tool. These are signs to mention, not a test. Having some doesn’t mean you have sleep apnea, and signs vary, so a short list doesn’t rule it out. A sleep study is how it’s diagnosed. If you’ve nodded off, or nearly, while driving, read <link>Driving & Staying Safe</link> now.

figure.printHeading: Questions to bring to your doctor

questions.1: Could these signs be sleep apnea, or something else?
questions.2: Do I need a sleep study? In a lab, or at home?
questions.3: How long is the wait, and who will contact me?
questions.4: Is it safe for me to drive while I wait?
questions.5: Will the kind of test matter for funding later?

5.title: Trouble falling or staying asleep?

items.1: Trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, with distress or daytime problems for 3 months or more, is called insomnia disorder
items.2: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment, before sleeping pills
items.3: CBT-I is usually 4 to 8 sessions with a trained clinician, in person or by video. Some people start with a self-guided program, online or from a book
items.4: Sleepwell, a not-for-profit program led from Dalhousie University, has CBT-I tools such as a sleep diary
items.5: Poor sleep can also come from sleep apnea. A sleep study may be needed if your doctor suspects it
items.6: Adults aged 18 to 64 need 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night. Adults 65 and older need 7 to 8

5.note: This site doesn’t cover insomnia in depth. Your doctor or nurse practitioner can assess it with you.

chips.1: Talk to your doctor or nurse practitioner

2.detail: Sleepwell is a not-for-profit program led from Dalhousie University.

6.title: More than snoring?

items.1: Loud snoring is a sign that your airway is partly blocked as you sleep
items.2: International guidance: most people with sleep apnea snore, but not everyone who snores has sleep apnea
items.3: Snoring with pauses in breathing, gasping or choking is a reason to see your doctor
items.4: So is snoring along with daytime sleepiness or tiredness, especially if you also have high blood pressure
items.5: Children can snore without having sleep apnea too. Signs and testing for children are in This Might Be You

6.note: Only a sleep study can tell snoring from sleep apnea. The checklist above can help you talk to your doctor.

7.title: Talking to your doctor

items.1: If you think you have sleep apnea, see your family doctor or nurse practitioner
items.2: Expect questions about your sleep, your daytime sleepiness and your health, and a look at your nose, mouth and throat
items.3: You may be asked to fill in a short questionnaire about daytime sleepiness
items.4: Expect to be asked whether you drive for work or have a safety-critical job, and about any near misses at the wheel
items.5: Then your doctor orders a home sleep test or refers you to a sleep clinic. How this works differs by province
items.6: Waits can be long. The Canadian target (2011) is testing within 4 weeks of referral for suspected severe sleep apnea, a safety-critical job or some serious health conditions, and within 6 months for everyone
items.7: In a 2009 survey, nearly 1 in 4 adults (23%) who had been told they had sleep apnea had never been referred for an overnight sleep test

7.note: Funding programs can have rules about testing. In Ontario, funding for a machine through the Assistive Devices Program starts with a doctor at an ADP-registered sleep clinic. The Non-Insured Health Benefits program doesn’t pay for sleep tests. Funding & Coverage has the details for your province.

8.title: Lab or home test?

items.1: An in-lab sleep study (polysomnography, or Level 1) is an overnight test in a sleep lab
items.2: Small wires on your head, face, chest and legs record your brain activity, breathing and oxygen as you sleep. Staff watch through the night
items.3: It’s the standard test. It can find every type of sleep apnea, and other sleep problems
items.4: A home sleep apnea test is a small device you wear overnight in your own bed, after someone shows you how to put it on
items.5: It records your breathing, oxygen and pulse. It can’t measure sleep, so it’s less sensitive than a lab study
items.6: It checks only for obstructive sleep apnea, in adults with symptoms whose doctor thinks it’s likely
items.7: Home tests aren’t for checking people who have no symptoms
items.8: A negative or unclear home test doesn’t rule out sleep apnea. If your doctor still suspects it, a lab study is the next step
items.9: Overnight oximetry, a clip that measures oxygen and pulse, isn’t enough on its own to diagnose sleep apnea
items.10: Your doctor chooses the test. Serious heart or lung disease, a past stroke, other sleep problems, regular opioid use and some other conditions mean a home test isn’t the right test. Your doctor refers you to a sleep specialist instead

8.note: For children, an overnight lab study is the standard. A home test is a second choice, only for healthy children over 5 who can’t get a lab study. More in This Might Be You.

9.title: Your results: the AHI

items.1: Your sleep study report says whether you have sleep apnea, and whether it’s mild, moderate or severe
items.2: The main number is the AHI (apnea-hypopnea index): how many times an hour your breathing stops or becomes shallow
items.3: Under 5 an hour is normal
items.4: Mild is 5 to 14 an hour, moderate is 15 to 29, and severe is 30 or more
items.5: The AHI isn’t the whole picture. Your sleep doctor also weighs your symptoms, your health and your job
items.6: Treatment may be suggested even when the AHI is mild, if you’re tired or sleepy
items.7: Once you’re on CPAP, the machine shows “events per hour”. It’s a useful daily guide, but not a true AHI. Ask your sleep team what yours means

9.note: This scale helps you read a report, not test yourself. Your sleep doctor goes over your results with you.

scale.heading: AHI: breathing events per hour of sleep
scale.adultsNote: These bands are for adults (19 and over).
scale.teamNote: Your sleep doctor also weighs your symptoms and your health.

10.title: What happens next

items.1: A sleep doctor or your own doctor reads your results, makes the diagnosis and suggests a treatment
items.2: The choice depends on how severe it is, your symptoms, your health and your job
items.3: CPAP is generally the most effective treatment. A machine blows a steady stream of air through a mask, to keep your airway open
items.4: Other options include an oral appliance for mild to moderate sleep apnea. Healthy eating, exercise and weight loss are recommended for people who carry extra weight, but they aren’t enough on their own if you’re sleepy or your sleep apnea is moderate or severe. Your Treatment Options covers each one
items.5: You need a prescription for CPAP. Your prescriber sets your settings
items.6: Expect follow-up: soon after you start, to check the treatment is working, then over the long term

10.note: Starting CPAP walks you through setup and the first weeks.

11.title: Who to ask

items.1: Your family doctor or nurse practitioner: your symptoms, a home test or a referral
items.2: A sleep doctor (sleep specialist): your diagnosis, how severe it is, and your treatment
items.3: A registered respiratory therapist (RRT): choosing and using your equipment, once your treatment is prescribed
items.4: Sleepy at the wheel, or nodded off while driving: read Driving & Staying Safe now

11.note: Not sure where to start? Start with your family doctor or nurse practitioner.

programsBand.heading: From first signs to a plan

1.heading: Notice
1.body: You, or someone who sleeps near you, notices snoring, pauses or gasping, or you’re sleepy all day. The checklist helps you list what you’ve noticed.

2.heading: Talk to your doctor
2.body: Your family doctor or nurse practitioner asks about your sleep and your health, and checks your nose, mouth and throat.

3.heading: Get tested
3.body: An overnight test, in a sleep lab or at home. Your doctor chooses which.

4.heading: Results and a plan
4.body: Your report gives a severity, from mild to severe. Your doctor or sleep doctor suggests a treatment.

closing.heading: Notice it, then ask
closing.body: You don’t have to work it out alone. Notice the signs, take your list to your doctor, and let a sleep study give the answer.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice. It can’t tell you whether you have sleep apnea, and it doesn’t replace care from your doctor or sleep team. Only a sleep study can diagnose sleep apnea, and your prescriber decides your treatment and its settings.

staying-safe.title: Driving & Staying Safe
staying-safe.heroBody: Sleepiness and driving, who decides about your licence, and how to keep your machine and mask safe. The signs that can’t wait come first.

categoriesIntro.eyebrow: On the road, or about your device?
categoriesIntro.heading: Safe driving, safe equipment
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter explains the rules and the safety steps. Your doctor and your licensing authority make the decisions about driving. Only your sleep team changes your treatment.

urgent.heading: Stop and act now
urgent.intro: Most of this chapter can wait. These can’t.

emergency.label: Call 911 now
emergency.lead: Call 911 or your local emergency number right away for:

signs.1: Chest pain or discomfort, or other signs of a heart attack
signs.2: Signs of a stroke: a drooping face, not being able to raise both arms, or slurred or jumbled speech
signs.4: Someone who has passed out, can’t be woken up, or is confused
signs.6: A child with severe trouble breathing, chest pain, blue lips or fingertips, or who is confused or not responding as usual. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department right away

stop.label: Stop now, then tell your doctor

signs.1: You fell asleep at the wheel, or nearly did, or had a crash because you were sleepy. Stop driving now and tell your doctor. You may also need to tell your licensing authority. Don’t drive again until your sleep apnea is treated and you’re told you can

soon.label: Not an emergency, but don’t wait

signs.1: You, or someone who sleeps near you, notice pauses in breathing, gasping or choking in your sleep. Talk to your doctor or health care provider as soon as you can. If someone can’t be woken up, call 911

urgent.note: Snoring and long pauses in breathing while a child sleeps can be signs of sleep apnea. Talk to your child’s health-care provider. <link>Chapter 06 covers children.</link>

startHere.heading: On the road, or about your device?

1.title: Sleepiness and driving

items.1: Untreated sleep apnea raises your risk of a car crash
items.2: The main sign is being sleepier than expected during the day
items.3: Most people with sleep apnea never have a crash. The risk is still higher
items.4: Your doctor may ask your licence class, and whether your work is one where sleepiness could be a hazard
items.5: Your doctor may also ask if you’ve fallen asleep at the wheel or come close in the past 5 years, and about any crashes or near misses when sleepy

1.note: A driver with sleep apnea can be found fit to drive again, based on their symptoms and on showing they use their treatment. If you’ve been sleepy at the wheel, see “Stop now, then tell your doctor” at the top of this page.

2.title: Who decides if you can drive

items.1: Your doctor assesses whether you’re medically fit to drive
items.2: The licensing authority where you live decides whether you can hold a licence. Driving safety is a provincial matter, not a federal one
items.3: How severe your sleep apnea is doesn’t decide it on its own. Sleepiness, other health conditions, medicines, your sleep schedule and past crashes count too
items.4: The rules differ from province to province
items.5: In Ontario, doctors and nurse practitioners must report sleep apnea that is untreated or not successfully treated, with an AHI of 30 or more and daytime sleepiness. A mandatory report leads to a licence suspension
items.6: In BC, drivers with sleep apnea have a licence condition: stop driving and report any episode of sleep at the wheel to their doctor and to RoadSafetyBC

2.note: AHI is the number of breathing pauses and shallow breaths per hour of sleep. Chapter 01 explains it. Ask your doctor how the rules apply to you.

3.title: What’s checked, by licence class

items.1: Every class: severe sleep apnea (AHI 30 or more) rules out driving unless it’s successfully treated, or a sleep specialist finds a low risk of a sleep-related crash
items.2: Every class: after a crash from falling asleep or sleepiness in the past 5 years, you must show your sleep apnea is successfully treated
items.3: In BC, treatment is checked with a full download from your CPAP or bilevel machine prepared by a respiratory therapist, or with a sleep study
items.4: Every class, if you use CPAP: machine records showing use of at least 4 hours a night, on more than 70% of nights, over at least 30 days
items.5: Private licences: your sleep doctor or your family doctor can confirm you’re fit to drive again
items.6: Commercial licences: the checks are stricter than for private drivers. Commercial drivers should ideally be seen at a sleep centre within 4 weeks of referral
items.7: Commercial licences: after a crash from falling asleep, or excessive sleepiness while driving, stop driving now until sleep tests are done and treatment works

3.note: These are licensing measures, not health targets. Your sleep team sets your own goal. Never change your machine’s settings to change your numbers.

figure.measureNote: These are licensing measures, not health targets. Your sleep team sets your own goal.
figure.decides: Your licensing authority makes the decision. Rules differ by province.

4.title: While you start treatment

items.1: While treatment starts, you may be able to keep driving if you aren’t sleepy while driving and haven’t had a crash from falling asleep. Ask your doctor
items.2: If you have been sleepy at the wheel or had a sleep-related crash, driving can start again once you use your treatment well and the sleepiness is gone
items.3: Your machine records how many hours and days you use it. Your doctor, an insurer or a licensing authority may ask for this report
items.4: Once treatment works, driving safely is your responsibility. Have your treatment reviewed from time to time by your doctor or sleep specialist, for example at least every 5 years
items.5: If sleepiness at the wheel comes back, stop driving and tell your doctor

4.note: Your machine’s settings are changed only by trained professionals. If your treatment isn’t working, call your sleep team.

5.title: Recalls: what to do

items.1: In 2021, Philips Respironics recalled several models of CPAP and bilevel machines. Sound-reducing foam inside them could break down, and particles could get into the air you breathe
items.2: If your machine is recalled, don’t stop or change your therapy before you talk to your doctor or equipment provider
items.3: Don’t try to remove or replace the foam yourself
items.4: Clean the machine only the way the maker’s instructions say. Ozone cleaning may make the foam break down faster
items.5: Some masks with magnets have also been recalled. See the next card

5.note: The maker planned to close its registration portal at the end of December 2024, and to finish its repair and replacement program in Canada by the end of June 2025. If you still use an affected machine, talk to your doctor or equipment provider.

6.title: Masks with magnets

items.1: Some CPAP masks have magnets in the clips or straps that hold the headgear on
items.2: Close to some metal implants and medical devices, a magnet may affect how they work or move them out of place. This could cause serious injury, or even death
items.3: It matters for everyone close to the mask: you, the people you live with, caregivers and bed partners
items.4: Implants that magnets may affect include pacemakers, defibrillators (ICDs), nerve stimulators (including hypoglossal nerve stimulators), brain fluid shunts, aneurysm clips, embolic coils, metal stents, implanted ports and pumps such as insulin pumps, hearing implants with a magnet such as cochlear implants, and metal in the eye. The full list is longer
items.5: What to do depends on the mask and on the implant. If you, or anyone close to the mask, has an implant or metal in their body, check with the mask’s maker and with your health care team about that implant before you use a mask with magnets
items.6: Some masks are named in Health Canada notices. For the masks in the 2022 public advisory, the advice is to stop using the mask if anyone close to it has one of the listed implants, and to get a mask without magnets. For an implant that isn’t on the list, keep the mask at least 15 cm (6 inches) away from it
items.7: For the masks in the 2022 advisory: if no one close to the mask has a metal implant or metal object in their body, you can keep using it

6.note: Not sure whether your mask has magnets? Check its instructions, or ask its maker. You can also look up your mask on the Government of Canada’s <link>recalls and safety alerts</link> site.

7.title: Cleaning the approved way

items.1: Clean your machine and mask only the way the maker’s instructions say
items.2: For the machines in the 2021 Philips recall, the advice was to stop using cleaning methods the maker hasn’t approved, such as ozone or UV-light cleaners
items.3: Ozone cleaning can speed up the breakdown of the foam inside some machines
items.4: Breathing ozone may affect how well your lungs work. UV light may badly burn skin and eyes
items.5: There isn’t enough evidence that all ozone and UV devices sold to kill germs are safe to use, or that they work

7.note: Everyday cleaning with pure soap and warm water is in Chapter 05.

8.title: Buying a device safely

items.1: Use CPAP only if you have a prescription from your doctor
items.2: Auto (APAP) and bilevel machines are more complex, and should be prescribed only by a sleep specialist
items.3: PAP machines sold in Canada must have a Health Canada medical device licence. You can check a device in the Medical Devices Active Licence Listing (MDALL)
items.4: Buying online can mean getting a device that is unlicensed, recalled or fake
items.5: Don’t buy from a website that won’t give a street address or a working phone number
items.6: Second-hand equipment: make sure it’s clean and works as it should. Every machine must be set for the person using it

8.note: Ask your health care provider whether a device is right for you before you buy, and follow up afterwards to check it fits and works.

9.title: Choosing a supplier

items.1: Choose a supplier with a registered respiratory therapist or a registered sleep technologist to guide you
items.2: A good supplier fits your mask, lets you try masks, and helps if you have trouble
items.3: New users can expect follow-up at about 7 days, an overnight oxygen test at 2 to 4 weeks, and check-ins at 30 and 60 days with a review of your machine’s data
items.4: In Ontario, you have the right to choose your community respiratory therapy provider. A respiratory therapist must tell you that you can choose another supplier, and that your care won’t suffer if you do
items.5: Many machines store your data on servers outside Canada, where privacy laws may be different. Ask your supplier how your data is handled

9.note: Bring the questions below when you choose a supplier.

fields.1: Who will fit my mask, and are they a respiratory therapist or sleep technologist?
fields.2: Can I try masks, and what is your exchange policy?
fields.3: When will you follow up with me?
fields.4: Where is my machine’s data stored, and who can see it?
fields.5: Is this device licensed by Health Canada?

10.title: Reporting a device problem

items.1: A device problem includes a device that fails, or stops working as well as it should
items.2: Everyone who has a problem with a medical device, or sees one, is strongly encouraged to report it to Health Canada
items.3: Consumers can report online with Health Canada’s consumer form
items.4: Your health care provider can help you report, and may add details that help the review
items.5: You can also report side effects or complaints about a recalled device to Health Canada

10.note: If the problem has made you unwell, call your doctor first.

items.1: Your doctor or sleep specialist: sleepiness at the wheel, fitness to drive, a recalled machine, a mask with magnets near an implant, or treatment that isn’t working
items.2: Your licensing authority: questions about your licence and the rules where you live
items.3: Your equipment provider: mask fit, how your equipment works, cleaning, and follow-up
items.4: Health Canada: report a problem with a medical device
items.5: Call 911: chest pain, signs of a stroke, trouble breathing, someone who has passed out or can’t be woken up, or anyone hurt in a crash. 911, or the nearest emergency department: a child with severe trouble breathing, chest pain, blue lips or fingertips, or who is confused or not responding as usual

5.label: 911 (for a child, 911 or the emergency department)

1.heading: Is it licensed?
1.body: PAP machines sold in Canada must have a Health Canada licence. Search the device in MDALL.

2.heading: Is it recalled?
2.body: If it is, don’t stop or change your therapy before you talk to your doctor or equipment provider.

3.heading: Magnets near an implant?
3.body: If your mask has magnets and anyone close to you has a metal implant, check with your health care team and the mask’s maker. If a Health Canada notice for your mask says to stop using it, stop.

4.heading: Cleaned the approved way?
4.body: Clean it only the way the maker’s instructions say.

closing.heading: Safe on the road, safe at home
closing.body: Use your treatment, know who decides about driving, and check your equipment: licensed, not recalled, magnets checked if anyone close to you has an implant, cleaned the approved way.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical or legal advice. Your doctor assesses your fitness to drive, and your licensing authority decides. Only your prescriber decides your treatment and settings, and only trained professionals change them. Liivv never advises on machine settings.

treatment-options.title: Your Treatment Options
treatment-options.heroBody: A breathing machine, a mouth device, or changes to everyday habits: what each one is, who it suits, and what to ask before you choose.
treatment-options.focus: Breathing machines: CPAP and APAP, bilevel, central and complex sleep apnea, travel machines, and renting, trying or buying. Without a machine: oral appliances, weight and everyday habits, comparing your options, shop fixes and new treatments, and who to ask.
treatment-options.vibe: Clear and even-handed: every option, with its trade-offs.

categoriesIntro.heading: The right treatment is the one you can use every night
categoriesIntro.body: Your sleep team chooses your treatment with you, based on your sleep test and your health. This chapter explains the options so you can ask good questions. Liivv never advises on machine settings. For a child, see This Might Be You.

startHere.heading: A breathing machine, or another way?

1.title: CPAP and APAP: the usual first treatment

items.1: CPAP is generally the most effective treatment for obstructive sleep apnea
items.2: A machine blows a steady stream of air through a tube into a mask. The air holds your airway open while you sleep
items.3: CPAP gives one steady pressure all night. APAP (auto CPAP) changes the pressure through the night as your breathing changes
items.4: You need a prescription. Your prescriber sets the pressure, and only trained professionals should change the machine’s settings
items.5: Each machine is set for the person using it. Using a machine set for someone else could harm your health
items.6: CPAP is a treatment, not a cure. It only works on the nights you use it

1.note: Fixed CPAP is the main treatment. APAP is an alternative, but not for people with heart or lung disease, nerve or muscle disease, or breathing problems in sleep that aren’t only obstructive, such as central sleep apnea. APAP is more complex than CPAP, and some guidance says only a sleep specialist should prescribe it. Your prescriber decides which one you get.

2.title: Bilevel (BiPAP)

items.1: A bilevel machine gives a higher pressure when you breathe in and a lower pressure when you breathe out
items.2: For obstructive sleep apnea, the main reason to use one is comfort: some people find it easier to breathe out against a lower pressure
items.3: Bilevel machines are more complex than CPAP. They should be prescribed only by a sleep specialist
items.4: Bilevel is also used for some other breathing problems in sleep, when oxygen and carbon dioxide levels don’t improve with CPAP
items.5: Government funding may help some people pay for bilevel. Ask your sleep team, and see Paying for it

2.note: Canadian guidance differs on when bilevel is used for obstructive sleep apnea. Your sleep specialist decides whether it’s right for you.

3.title: Central and complex sleep apnea: a specialist’s call

items.1: In central sleep apnea, the throat and airway are normal. The brain doesn’t send the signal to breathe
items.2: It is common in people with heart failure, atrial fibrillation or other heart conditions, people taking opioids, and people with some neurological conditions
items.3: Standard PAP machines are not meant to be the only treatment for central sleep apnea. Used alone, they can make it worse
items.4: If central sleep apnea is suspected, it should be checked with a detailed overnight sleep test in an accredited sleep lab, to find the right treatment
items.5: Treating the other condition, such as heart failure, can improve central sleep apnea
items.6: Some people start having central pauses after they begin CPAP. This is called complex sleep apnea, and it can happen in up to 10% of people treated with CPAP. If it happens to you, talk with your doctor about continuing PAP

3.note: Some newer machines, such as adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV), are used for central sleep apnea. In 2015, Health Canada posted a Type I recall of several ASV machines: a serious safety concern was found in people with symptomatic, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, whose risk of cardiovascular death was 33.5% higher on ASV. ASV is a sleep specialist’s decision. If you have heart failure, make sure your sleep specialist knows.

4.title: Travel machines

items.1: Smaller travel machines are easy to carry, quiet, and can run on batteries
items.2: The trade-offs: the pressure may not stay as steady, batteries cost extra where there’s no power outlet, and they may not humidify the air enough
items.3: Altitude can change how a machine works, unless it adjusts for it. Tell your provider if you live in, or often travel to, places much higher or lower than where your pressure was set
items.4: Most machines can also run on a battery pack, a car adapter or a marine battery adapter
items.5: A travel machine still needs a prescription, set by your prescriber for you
items.6: Keep using your treatment when you travel. Flying? See Everyday Liivving for taking your machine on board

4.note: Talk to your prescriber and equipment provider before you choose a travel machine, so it fits your prescription and the way you travel.

5.title: Renting, trying or buying

items.1: You can buy or rent CPAP equipment
items.2: Ask about a trial. Some suppliers offer equipment trials, and some won’t take back or refund equipment once it has been used
items.3: If you end up needing a different machine, an extended health insurer may refuse to pay for a second one. That’s one more reason a trial matters
items.4: Look for a supplier with a registered respiratory therapist or a registered polysomnographic technologist to support you
items.5: Equipment bought in Canada usually has a 3-year warranty. Ask about warranty, how long repairs take, and whether you get a loaner in the meantime
items.6: Every PAP machine sold in Canada needs a Health Canada medical device licence. You can check a machine in Health Canada’s licence list
items.7: A second-hand machine is hard to judge. It may not work well, and the warranty may be gone
items.8: You can choose your supplier. In Ontario, respiratory therapists must tell you that you can pick another provider or product, and that your care won’t suffer if you do

5.note: Whoever you buy from, online or in person: if you’re new to PAP, look for a provider who shows you how to use your equipment, teaches you about PAP therapy and checks in with you regularly. If you buy online, choose a company that asks for your prescription first. Some local providers won’t help with equipment bought online.

6.title: Oral appliances

items.1: An oral appliance fits over your teeth. It holds your lower jaw and tongue forward so they don’t block your airway
items.2: It may suit mild to moderate sleep apnea, or people who can’t use or don’t want CPAP
items.3: Get a medical assessment first, to confirm sleep apnea and how severe it is. Your dentist should work with your doctor
items.4: See a dentist with experience fitting these devices. For people it works for, a custom device can work as well as CPAP and is often easier to put up with
items.5: Adjustable devices are better than fixed ones. Devices with rigid bars or screws likely work better than ones with elastic straps
items.6: Boil-and-bite devices are not recommended for treating sleep apnea. They are much less effective and more likely to cause problems
items.7: Jaw or tooth pain, chewing trouble and some tooth movement can happen. Tell your dentist if it isn’t comfortable
items.8: After you start, your doctor may order a follow-up sleep test to check it’s working

6.note: An oral appliance is a medical treatment, not a store-bought snoring guard. Your sleep team and your dentist decide together if it’s right for you.

7.title: Weight and everyday habits

items.1: Mild sleep apnea with overweight or obesity: lifestyle changes are the recommended treatment
items.2: Mild sleep apnea without overweight: active treatment isn’t routinely recommended. But treatment should be considered if you’re tired or sleepy, even when it’s mild
items.3: Healthy habits help, but on their own they aren’t enough if you’re sleepy or have moderate or severe sleep apnea
items.4: Losing weight can shrink the tissue around your airway. People who lose 10% of their weight can have a 30% decrease in their symptoms
items.5: Weight loss works better if you keep using your treatment while you lose weight, then get retested once you reach your goal
items.6: Alcohol and sedatives (medicines that make you sleepy) can relax your throat muscles too much and let your airway close. Avoiding them may help keep it open
items.7: Smoking can make your nose stuffy and irritated, which can get in the way of CPAP
items.8: Lifestyle changes don’t work for everyone, and may not work forever. If your symptoms come back, see your doctor
items.9: If you gain or lose 30 pounds (about 14 kg) or more, go back to your sleep specialist. Your pressure may need to be checked

7.note: Habits work alongside your treatment, not instead of it, unless your sleep team says so. Don’t stop a treatment or a prescribed medicine without talking to your doctor.

8.title: Comparing your options

items.1: Moderate or severe sleep apnea: CPAP is the recommended treatment. If CPAP isn’t acceptable to you, an oral appliance is recommended
items.2: Mild sleep apnea: lifestyle changes if you’re overweight. CPAP or an oral appliance are also options
items.3: CPAP has the largest effect on how severe sleep apnea is
items.4: A jaw-advancing oral appliance has roughly a 70% chance of working in mild sleep apnea. In moderate sleep apnea it has about a 50% chance of fully working, and in severe about 40%. In moderate and severe, the chances are lower with a BMI over 35
items.5: Every treatment takes getting used to. Using it every night, all night, is what makes it work
items.6: Whatever you choose, follow-up continues until your breathing pauses are back to normal: fewer than 5 an hour
items.7: Tongue-retaining devices are only for snoring or very mild sleep apnea

8.note: Your sleep team decides with you, based on your sleep test, your health and what you can use every night.

9.title: Shop fixes and new treatments: check first

items.1: Nasal strips and nasal dilators may help air flow through your nose. They don’t treat the blockage in your throat that causes sleep apnea
items.2: A chin strap on its own doesn’t fix the blockage either. A badly fitted strap can push the jaw back and make the blockage worse
items.3: Boil-and-bite mouthguards are not recommended for treating sleep apnea
items.4: There are many experimental treatments. Before you try one, ask your sleep specialist about the risks and benefits for you

9.note: Snoring can be a sign of sleep apnea. If you’re treating snoring on your own, get checked first.

items.1: Your prescriber or sleep specialist: which treatment, which machine, and your pressure
items.2: A dentist with experience in oral appliances: after your medical assessment
items.3: Your equipment provider’s respiratory therapist: set-up, mask fit, and trouble getting used to your machine
items.4: Your doctor: if your symptoms come back, or your weight changes by 30 pounds or more

1.heading: Why this treatment?
1.body: Ask your prescriber why they chose it for you, and what else could work.

2.heading: Can I try it first?
2.body: Ask about trials, whether used equipment can be returned, and what your insurer will pay for.

3.heading: Who helps me after?
3.body: Look for a registered respiratory therapist or polysomnographic technologist, and check-ins in the first weeks.

4.heading: Is it licensed?
4.body: Every PAP machine sold in Canada needs a Health Canada medical device licence. You can look it up.

closing.heading: One step at a time
closing.body: Most people start with one treatment and adjust with their sleep team. Asking questions is part of getting it right.

starting-cpap.title: Starting CPAP
starting-cpap.heroBody: Getting set up and getting used to it: your prescription, your mask, water for the humidifier, the first nights, and who to call when something isn’t right.
starting-cpap.focus: Your setup: follow-up, your prescription, mask types, fit, the humidifier and a starter list. The first weeks: first nights, what your usage numbers mean, fixes for common problems, and what to do if it isn’t working.
starting-cpap.vibe: Practical and patient. Most problems have a fix, and you don’t have to solve them alone.

categoriesIntro.heading: Your first weeks with CPAP
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter helps you follow the plan your sleep team made with you. Your prescriber sets your pressure. Liivv never advises on settings. If your team told you something different, follow your team.

startHere.heading: Getting set up, or getting used to it?

1.title: Setup and follow-up

items.1: Wherever you get your equipment, online or in person, a good start includes a mask fitting, help using your machine, and someone who follows up to see how your therapy is going
items.2: About 7 days in: a check on mask comfort, the airflow, leaks, how often you use it, and any feeling of being closed in
items.3: At 2 to 4 weeks: an overnight oxygen test while you use CPAP, to check your oxygen level is normal on treatment
items.4: At 30 and 60 days: the same questions, plus how you sleep and feel, and a look at your machine’s data to see if treatment is working
items.5: After that: a follow-up at least once a year, with your machine’s data and a check of your mask and tubing

1.note: This schedule comes from Canadian provincial guidance for people new to CPAP. It’s shown here for every province. Your sleep team may set a different one. If so, follow theirs.

2.title: Your prescription and settings

items.1: You need a prescription for CPAP. It comes after a medical assessment and a sleep test
items.2: Your prescription says what pressure your machine is set to. For insurance, it should also name your mask and humidifier
items.3: Auto-adjusting machines (APAP) and bilevel machines are more complex. A sleep specialist should prescribe them
items.4: Only trained professionals should change your machine’s settings. Don’t change them yourself
items.5: A machine is set for one person. Using a machine set for someone else could harm your health
items.6: Ask your prescriber about your pressure if your weight goes up or down by 30 pounds or more, or if you move to, or often travel to, a much higher or lower place. If you’re told you have central sleep apnea, talk to your doctor about whether to keep using CPAP
items.7: Every CPAP machine sold in Canada must have a medical device licence. You can look a machine up in Health Canada’s online licence list
items.8: In Ontario, respiratory therapists must tell you that you can choose a different provider or product

2.note: Liivv never advises on pressure or settings. Questions about them go to your prescriber or your respiratory therapist.

3.title: Mask types to ask your RT about

items.1: Nasal pillows sit at the openings of your nostrils
items.2: A nasal mask fits over your nose
items.3: A full-face mask covers your nose and mouth
items.4: A child is fitted for a mask made for children (a paediatric mask), not an adult one
items.5: Some masks have magnets in the clips or straps. If you, or anyone you live or sleep near, has an implant or metal device that magnets can affect, such as a pacemaker, tell your RT before you choose a mask. Already using a mask with magnets? Check with the mask’s maker and your health care team about the implant

3.note: The right mask is the one that fits you and feels comfortable. It can make a big difference to how well CPAP works, and to whether you keep using it. These are general patterns, not a fitting. Try masks on with your RT.

questions.4: I have a beard or moustache
questions.5: I move around a lot in my sleep
questions.6: My nose is often stuffy or blocked
questions.7: I don’t want anything inside my nose
questions.8: I have a high, narrow bridge to my nose

reasons.1: A full-face mask may suit people who breathe through their mouth. So may a nasal mask with a chin strap.
reasons.2: Nasal masks and nasal pillows may suit people who breathe mainly through their nose.
reasons.3: Nasal pillows or a nasal mask may feel less closed in. Some people feel closed in with a full-face mask.
reasons.4: Nasal pillows may suit people with facial hair.
reasons.5: Nasal pillows may suit people who move around in their sleep. A chin strap may help keep a mask on.
reasons.6: A full-face mask may suit people whose nose is often stuffy or blocked.
reasons.7: If you don’t want anything inside your nose, a nasal mask may suit you better than pillows.
reasons.8: With a high, narrow nose bridge, nasal pillows may leak less than other masks.

figure.statusMany: {count} mask types fit what you ticked. All three stay listed.

Tell your RT if you, or anyone you live or sleep near, has an implant or metal device that magnets can affect, such as a pacemaker. Check with the mask’s maker and your health care team before you use a mask with magnets. More in <link>Driving & Staying Safe</link>.
figure.privacy: This doesn’t choose a mask for you. Nothing you tick is saved.

4.title: Getting the fit right

items.1: The top of the mask sits at the bridge of your nose. The bottom sits about halfway between the bottom of your nose and your upper lip
items.2: The smallest mask that fits is usually the best choice
items.3: A little leak is fine, as long as it isn’t blowing into your eyes. You shouldn’t need to pull the straps very tight
items.4: When you try masks, lie on your back and on each side, with the machine attached. Make sure the headgear is easy for you to use
items.5: Ask about a mask trial or an exchange before you buy. Some providers don’t take returns once a mask has been used
items.6: Marks should fade soon after you take the mask off. If they don’t, or your skin is sore, the straps may be too tight or the mask may not fit

4.note: For a child, don’t fasten the mask and straps too tightly. You should be able to slip two fingers under the strap. If the mask doesn’t seem the right size, ask your child’s home care company or sleep team about other masks.

5.title: Humidifier and distilled water

items.1: Most CPAP machines have a humidifier: a small water tank that adds moisture to the air
items.2: Moist air can help with a dry mouth or throat, a stuffy nose and nosebleeds
items.3: Use only distilled water. You can buy it at most grocery stores and pharmacies
items.4: Put in fresh water each night. Empty the tank before you move the machine, so no water spills into it
items.5: Don’t put a regular room humidifier in your bedroom. It could damage the CPAP machine’s motor
items.6: Water drops or popping sounds in the tube? A heated tube helps stop water collecting. Ask your RT
items.7: You may need more moisture in winter than in summer. Ask your RT, rather than changing the settings yourself

5.note: Your provider will show you how to fill the water tank. Cleaning is in Everyday Liivving.

items.1: Your machine, as prescribed, with its humidifier water chamber
items.2: A mask with headgear, fitted for you
items.3: Tubing, standard or heated
items.4: Filters for your machine: disposable, reusable, or both
items.5: A chin strap, if your mouth falls open as you sleep
items.6: Distilled water

7.title: Your first nights

items.1: Some people sleep well with CPAP from the first night. Others need time to get used to the mask and the pressure. It can take up to 6 weeks
items.2: Practise first. Wear the mask for short periods during the day, sitting up and awake, before you sleep in it
items.3: Wear it the whole time you sleep, every night. You can wear it for naps too
items.4: Knocking the mask off now and then is normal. Put it back on and keep your treatment going all night
items.5: Many people feel less sleepy within about 2 weeks. The full benefit can take about 6 weeks
items.6: A bed partner may sleep better too. They can help by learning about your treatment

7.note: For a child, practise wearing the mask while they’re awake and doing a quiet activity they enjoy. Making it part of the bedtime routine, or a sticker chart, can help. More in This Might Be You.

8.title: What your usage numbers mean

items.1: Your machine records how many hours you use it, and on how many days
items.2: It may also show ‘events per hour’. That’s a useful daily sign of how therapy is going, but it isn’t the same as the AHI from a sleep test
items.3: Your prescriber, your insurer or a licensing body may ask for this data. When you choose a machine, ask whether it stores at least 200 days of it
items.4: Many machines store data on servers outside Canada, where privacy laws may be different. Ask your provider how your data is handled

8.note: The measures below are used by driver licensing bodies. They are not a health target. Your sleep team sets your goal.

figure.heading: Usage measures used for driver’s licences

driving.label: Driving, once treated
driving.value: At least 4 hours a night on more than 70% of nights, over at least 30 days, from your machine’s data
driving.foot: The licensing authority makes the decision. The rules for commercial drivers are stricter.

severe.label: Severe sleep apnea, any licence
severe.value: Severe sleep apnea (AHI 30 or more) must be successfully treated, unless a sleep specialist judges the risk of a crash low. In BC, proof of treatment can be a full report of your machine’s data prepared by a respiratory therapist, or a sleep study
severe.foot: The licensing authority makes the decision.

figure.always: None of these is a goal for your health. Ask your sleep team what your goal is.

items.1: Air leaking: a small leak that doesn’t blow into your eyes is fine. For more, check the fit and the size. Don’t over-tighten the straps
items.2: Dry mouth: your mouth may be falling open. A chin strap can help, and your doctor can tell you whether a full-face mask suits you. A pharmacist can suggest products for a dry mouth
items.3: Dry or stuffy nose: a humidifier can help. Still stuffy? See your doctor. It could be sinusitis, allergies or swelling in your nose
items.4: Bloating: tell your healthcare team. They may have ideas to help
items.5: Feeling closed in: practise wearing the mask while you’re awake. Nasal pillows or a nasal mask may feel less closed in than a full-face mask. Talking with a counsellor can help too
items.6: Marks or sore skin: the straps may be too tight, or the mask may not fit. Wash the mask every day, and wash and dry your face before you put it on. A rash? Call your doctor
items.7: Water in the tube, or popping sounds: ask your RT whether a heated tube would help. Empty the water tank before you move the machine
items.8: Mask coming off at night: now and then is normal. A chin strap may help keep it on
items.9: The air feels too strong, or it’s hard to breathe out: call your RT or prescriber. Don’t change the pressure or settings yourself
items.10: Still sleepy, even though you use it every night: have your supplier check that your machine is working, and talk to your sleep doctor. Sleepy while driving? Go to Driving & Staying Safe

figure.always: Whatever the problem, don’t change your pressure or settings yourself. Call your RT or prescriber.
figure.redFlagLink: Urgent signs, in Driving & Staying Safe

10.title: If you can’t get used to it

items.1: It can take a few weeks, or even months, to feel comfortable with a mask. Don’t give up
items.2: Go back to your RT or supplier. A different mask or a better fit often helps
items.3: Talk to your sleep doctor about any medical concerns. They can suggest tips or test for other problems
items.4: Feelings can make it harder to keep going. Talking with a counsellor, or support from others, can help
items.5: If CPAP still doesn’t work for you, your doctor may suggest another treatment, or a sleep specialist
items.6: If you stop using CPAP, your symptoms come back. Talk to your doctor before you stop

10.note: Other treatments are in Your Treatment Options.

11.title: Who to ask

items.1: Your prescriber or sleep doctor: your pressure and settings, symptoms, still feeling sleepy, central sleep apnea, and before you stop
items.2: Your respiratory therapist (RT) or CPAP provider: mask fitting and trials, using your machine, leaks and comfort, machine checks and data reviews
items.3: A health line: in BC call 8-1-1 (7-1-1 for the deaf and hard of hearing). In Alberta, call Health Link at 811, any time, day or night
items.4: Very sleepy at the wheel, or worried right now: the urgent signs in Driving & Staying Safe

11.note: Where it’s within their scope of practice, respiratory therapists can recommend your equipment once your prescriber has set your therapy and pressure.

1.heading: Prescription first
1.body: CPAP needs a prescription. Your prescriber sets your pressure.

2.heading: Settings stay with the professionals
2.body: Only trained professionals change your machine’s settings. Don’t change them yourself.

3.heading: Distilled water only
3.body: Fill the humidifier with distilled water, fresh each night.

4.heading: Keep going, and call
4.body: It can take up to 6 weeks to settle in. If something isn’t right, call your RT.

closing.heading: One night at a time
closing.body: Most people need some time and a few changes before CPAP feels normal. Ask for help early, keep your follow-ups, and keep going.

everyday-liivving.title: Everyday Liivving
everyday-liivving.heroBody: Cleaning your equipment, replacing worn parts, understanding your machine’s data, and taking CPAP with you: on a plane, on a trip or into hospital.
everyday-liivving.focus: Clean and replace: your cleaning routine, ozone and UV cleaners, when to replace supplies, signs a part is worn, caring for a child’s CPAP, and your machine’s data. Away from home: flying, a travel checklist, hospital stays, and who to ask.
everyday-liivving.vibe: Practical and steady: small habits that keep treatment working.

categoriesIntro.heading: Small habits keep your treatment working
categoriesIntro.body: Clean your equipment, replace parts when they wear out, and keep using your treatment wherever you sleep. Your owner’s manual comes first. This chapter puts general advice beside it. Liivv never advises on machine settings.

1.title: Your cleaning routine

items.1: Your owner’s manual comes first. It tells you how to care for your model
items.2: Clean your mask every day. Wash it with pure soap and warm water
items.3: Skip soaps with bleach, chlorine, alcohol, moisturizers, scents or antibacterial agents
items.4: Rinse the mask in plain water. You can add plain white vinegar to the rinse water: it cuts down on smells and germs
items.5: Let the mask air dry. Keep it out of direct sunlight
items.6: Every week, hand wash the tubing and headgear with pure soap and warm water. Gently towel dry them, then let them air dry
items.7: If you use a humidifier, use distilled water and replace the water each night. Clean the humidifier as your manual says
items.8: Empty the humidifier before you move your machine, so water doesn’t spill into it
items.9: Wash your face and dry it well before you put the mask on

1.note: Don’t put a regular room humidifier in your bedroom: it could damage your CPAP machine’s motor. Ask your equipment provider how to keep your model clean and working well.

2.title: Ozone and UV cleaners

items.1: Clean your machine only with the methods in its instructions
items.2: For the machines in the 2021 Philips recall, the advice was to stop using cleaners that use ozone or ultraviolet (UV) light, because they aren’t authorized cleaning methods
items.3: In some recalled machines, ozone cleaning may make the sound-reducing foam inside break down faster
items.4: Breathing in ozone from ozone-generating devices may harm how your lungs work and irritate your airways

2.note: Have a machine in the Philips foam recall? Don’t stop or change how you use it on your own. Talk to your doctor or equipment provider first. Recalls are covered in Driving & Staying Safe.

3.title: When to replace supplies

items.1: Start with your manual. Parts need replacing at different times, based on the maker’s advice and how you use them
items.2: As a general range, most machines are replaced every 3 to 5 years, and accessories every 3 to 12 months
items.3: The parts you replace from time to time: the mask, tubing, humidifier water chamber, chin strap and filters
items.4: Change the machine’s filter every 2 months, or as needed
items.5: If a plan pays for your equipment, check its replacement time frames before you order
items.6: Programs set the most they will pay for over a period of time. Those limits are about funding, not a health schedule
items.7: In Ontario, the Assistive Devices Program helps pay for the machine package, but not replacement masks or headgear. ODSP can cover replacement supplies for people who receive it, once the ministry approves the need

3.note: Choosing a new mask? Some masks have magnets that can affect certain metal implants, such as a pacemaker or a metal stent, in you or in anyone who lives with you, cares for you or shares your bed. If that might apply, check with the mask’s maker and your health care team before you order. Read the warning in Driving & Staying Safe.

4.title: Signs a part is worn

items.1: Check your tubing and headgear often. If they’re worn, get new ones
items.2: You shouldn’t have to pull the headgear very tight to stop leaks. If you can’t get a seal without large leaks, ask your provider about a different style of mask
items.3: Marks from the mask should fade soon after you take it off. If they don’t, or your skin is sore or red, the headgear may be too tight or the mask may not fit right
items.4: A small leak is fine, as long as it doesn’t blow into your eyes
items.5: Still sleepy even though you use CPAP every night? First make sure your equipment is working: your supplier can check it. Then talk to your sleep doctor
items.6: If you gain or lose 30 pounds or more, see your doctor. Your pressure may need to be changed, and a mask may no longer meet your needs
items.7: Machine not working properly? Call your provider. Equipment bought in Canada usually has a 3-year warranty. Ask about a loaner while yours is checked or repaired
items.8: You can report a problem with a medical device to Health Canada

4.note: Programs don’t pay to replace lost equipment or equipment damaged by misuse. Store and pack yours with care.

5.title: Caring for a child’s CPAP

items.1: Your child’s equipment provider (home care company) will give you instructions for your child’s machine. Follow those first
items.2: Clean your child’s mask each morning. Oils from your child’s skin can break down the mask
items.3: Wash the mask by hand with warm water and a mild soap. Let it air dry: don’t dry it with a towel or tissue
items.4: Wash the headgear by hand with mild soap and water once a week, and let it air dry
items.5: If the mask doesn’t seem to be a good size, ask the equipment provider about other masks your child could use
items.6: If an error message shows on your child’s CPAP machine, contact the equipment provider

5.note: If your child is sick and you’re worried about their breathing, contact your child’s health-care provider, or have your child seen at your local emergency department.

6.title: Your machine’s data and follow-ups

items.1: Many machines record how many hours you use them, pauses in your breathing, and air leaks
items.2: Some send this to a phone app and to your equipment provider. Others save it to a USB stick or SD card, if you’d rather not use Wi-Fi, cellular data or Bluetooth
items.3: Many machines show an “events per hour” number. It’s a useful daily sign of how well treatment is working, but it isn’t the same as a sleep test result
items.4: New users may expect check-ins: about 7 days after starting, an overnight oxygen test at 2 to 4 weeks, then 30 and 60 days, with a review of the machine’s data
items.5: After that, a yearly follow-up with a download of your machine’s data is recommended
items.6: Ideally, you use your treatment every night, all night
items.7: Your doctor, insurer or a licensing office may ask for this data. If you’ve been told not to drive, Canadian guidance looks for at least 4 hours a night on more than 70% of nights, over at least 30 days. That is a licensing measure, not a health target: your sleep team sets your goal
items.8: Ask your provider how your data is shared and stored. Many machines store data on servers outside Canada, where privacy laws may be different

6.note: Your sleep team reads your data and decides on any changes. Only trained professionals should change your machine’s settings. Liivv never advises on them.

7.title: Flying with CPAP

items.1: Your CPAP machine is allowed in carry-on and in checked baggage. Bring it as carry-on
items.2: At security, take the main unit out of its case and put it in a bin. You can put it in a clear plastic bag first: bring your own
items.3: The tubes and mask can stay in the case. Screening officers won’t touch the parts that connect to the tubes
items.4: The main unit may need extra screening, such as a swab test for explosives
items.5: Distilled water for your machine is exempt from the 100 ml liquid limit. Keep it in its own container and show it to the screening officer
items.6: You don’t need a medical document at security. If you think one would help, show it to the screening officer with your machine
items.7: Look for the Family and Accessible Line at security. If you have special medical needs, you can contact CATSA at least 48 hours before your flight
items.8: Tell your airline about your machine when you book. Ask about using it on board and about power
items.9: The usual limit of two carry-on bags doesn’t apply to medical equipment. Check your airline’s rules too

7.note: A letter from your doctor can make security go more smoothly. It should say your CPAP is needed for a medical condition, and list the model and serial number of all your equipment.

8.title: Travel checklist

items.1: Keep using your treatment while you’re away. Bring your CPAP everywhere you sleep
items.2: Your machine, mask and tubing, in your carry-on
items.3: Distilled water for the humidifier
items.4: A letter from your doctor, with the model and serial number of all your equipment
items.5: A converter, if the electricity is different where you’re going
items.6: Going somewhere much higher or lower than home? Ask your equipment provider first: altitude can change how some machines work
items.7: Your airline told about your machine when you booked

8.note: Going into hospital while you’re away? Bring your machine and use it.

this-might-be-you.title: This Might Be You
this-might-be-you.heroBody: Sleep apnea can look different in a child or a woman, and the risk grows with age. What to watch for, how children are tested and treated, and the help you can get.
this-might-be-you.focus: Seasons of life: signs in children, testing and treatment for children, a child on CPAP, later life, and women. Care and community: partners and household, helping someone, First Nations and Inuit coverage, and paying for it.
this-might-be-you.vibe: Warm and practical: for the person who notices, and the person who helps.

categoriesIntro.heading: Sleep apnea doesn’t look the same for everyone
categoriesIntro.body: Sleep apnea can look different in children and in women, and the risk grows with age. Often it’s a parent, partner or family member who notices first. This chapter helps you know what to look for and who to ask. It is not a way to diagnose anyone.

startHere.heading: A season of life, or someone you care for?

1.title: Signs in children

items.1: Sleep apnea affects 1 to 5 children in 100. Some children snore but don’t have sleep apnea
items.2: At night: snoring (steady, with pauses, or only in some positions), breathing only through the mouth, long pauses in breathing, waking often, and sweating
items.3: Restless sleep can look like turning from side to side, jerking the legs, or sitting up to breathe better while still asleep
items.4: During the day: sleepiness, especially at school or in quiet activities, trouble learning or concentrating, low energy for sports and hobbies, and irritability, hyperactivity, impulsivity or aggression
items.5: The most common cause is large tonsils or adenoids. This often happens between ages 2 and 8. Extra weight, weak breathing muscles, the shape of the skull and jaw, and other health conditions can also cause it
items.6: Other signs parents notice include bed-wetting, night terrors, and unusual sleep positions, such as the head tipped back or sitting up with the mouth open
items.7: Finding it early matters. Untreated, it can be linked to high blood pressure, poor growth, learning difficulties and behaviour problems

1.note: These signs are not a diagnosis. If you notice them, talk to your child’s doctor. Snoring and long pauses while your child sleeps are worth mentioning.

2.title: Testing for children

items.1: Start with your child’s doctor. They will usually refer your child to a sleep medicine specialist at a hospital
items.2: An overnight sleep study in a sleep lab (polysomnography) is the standard test for children. There is no replacement for it at this time
items.3: During the study, small wires are attached to the skin with paste and child-friendly tape. They don’t hurt. They record oxygen, breathing, heartbeat and sleep, and a sleep technologist watches through the night
items.4: A home sleep test may be a second option for otherwise healthy children over 5, when a lab study is out of reach because of long waits, distance or cost
items.5: Overnight oximetry (a finger sensor that measures oxygen) and questionnaires can help, but they shouldn’t be used alone to diagnose sleep apnea in children
items.6: Lab studies are hard to get in many parts of Canada, and waits can delay treatment. Ask your child’s doctor what the wait is where you live

2.note: Your child’s sleep specialist looks at the results to find what kind of sleep problem it is and how serious it is.

fields.1: Which sleep test is right for my child?
fields.2: How long is the wait, and where is the nearest lab?
fields.3: What should we bring to the sleep study?
fields.4: Who will explain the results to us?

3.title: Treatment for children

items.1: Surgery to remove the tonsils and adenoids (adenotonsillectomy) is often the first treatment, because large tonsils and adenoids are often the cause
items.2: Other treatments include a weight program if your child carries extra weight, medicines to reduce swelling in the nose or airway, and less exposure to second-hand smoke and other pollution
items.3: Some children need CPAP, a machine that blows air through a mask to keep the airway open. Some still need it after other treatments
items.4: After this surgery, children with sleep apnea are watched more closely in hospital. Most go home after one night. Children under 3 with other conditions, such as Down syndrome, are more likely to have breathing problems after surgery
items.5: Your child may need a follow-up sleep study after treatment
items.6: Once your child is home after surgery, call your child’s surgeon, clinic or doctor right away for a fever of 38.5°C or higher, vomiting that won’t stop, pain that gets worse, refusing to drink, or fresh blood in the nose or mouth
items.7: If your child is bleeding or having trouble breathing, take them to the closest emergency department right away

3.note: If your child has other health conditions, the sleep team may also bring in other specialists. Tonsil surgery isn’t used to treat snoring alone in children.

4.title: A child on CPAP

items.1: Your child’s sleep team follows your child’s care. A sleep study sets the pressure on the machine, and another study after starting checks that it’s working and whether the pressure needs to change
items.2: Your child needs a mask made for children (a paediatric mask), fitted and tried on, not an adult mask
items.3: CPAP and follow-up care are different for children. Get help from professionals who work with children
items.4: Your child can practise wearing the mask for short times during the day, during a quiet activity they enjoy
items.5: Most children need time to get used to it. Make it part of the bedtime routine. A sticker chart or other reward can help
items.6: Don’t fasten the mask too tightly. Check your child’s face for pressure marks
items.7: CPAP is for every night of sleep, including holidays, sleepovers and camping
items.8: If your child is sick and you’re worried about their breathing, call your child’s health-care provider or have your child seen at your local emergency department

4.note: Children’s CPAP gives one steady pressure, set by the sleep team. Auto-adjusting machines are not for children. Some masks with magnets, including a youth version of one mask, have had Health Canada warnings: see Partners and household.

5.title: Later life

items.1: In 2016 and 2017, 12.8% of Canadians aged 60 to 79 said they had been diagnosed with sleep apnea. That’s three times the rate in adults aged 18 to 59
items.2: Adults aged 40 to 79 are at higher risk than younger adults. Being over 40 is one of the risk factors
items.3: As you get older, or if you gain weight, habits that helped before may stop being enough. If your symptoms come back, see your doctor
items.4: If you gain or lose 30 pounds or more, see your doctor. Your treatment may need to be checked
items.5: Before sedation or anesthesia, for a dental procedure, a test or surgery, tell everyone caring for you that you have sleep apnea
items.6: Use your CPAP or dental device everywhere you sleep, including an overnight stay in hospital. A medical alert bracelet that says you have sleep apnea can help
items.7: In Ontario, residents of long-term care homes can get Assistive Devices Program funding for a PAP machine

5.note: These numbers come from a national health survey. They describe Canadians in general, not any one person.

6.title: Women: the signs can look different

items.1: In a 2016–2017 national survey, men were twice as likely as women to say they had been diagnosed with sleep apnea
items.2: Men more often have the classic signs, such as loud snoring or someone seeing them stop breathing
items.3: Women more often feel tired or sleepy in the day, or have trouble falling or staying asleep
items.4: Because the signs differ, sleep apnea may be missed in women

6.note: Always tired, or sleeping badly, and not sure why? Ask your doctor whether sleep apnea could be part of it. See Is It Sleep Apnea? for the signs.

7.title: Partners and household

items.1: Bed partners and family often notice the signs first. Many people with sleep apnea don’t know they snore or gasp for breath at night
items.2: Once your partner is treated, you may sleep better too
items.3: Some CPAP masks have magnets in the clips or straps. Their magnetic field may affect how some metal implants and objects in the body work, or move them. Examples are pacemakers, metal stents and metal in the eye. This may cause serious injury
items.4: For the masks in Health Canada’s 2022 advisory, the advice is to stop using the mask if you, anyone in your household, a caregiver or a bed partner has one of the listed implants, and to get a mask with no magnets. For other masks with magnets, check with the mask’s maker and your health care team
items.5: A later Health Canada recall of other masks with magnets warned that interference could affect how an implant works or where it sits, with a risk of serious injury or death
items.6: Each machine is set for the person using it. Using a machine set for someone else could harm your health

7.note: Does anyone in your home have a pacemaker, defibrillator, cochlear implant, metal stent, clip or plate, or any other implant? Check whether your mask has magnets, and check with the mask’s maker and your health care team before you use it.

8.title: Helping someone

items.1: If someone you love snores with pauses or gasps in their sleep, and is very sleepy in the day, encourage them to see their doctor
items.2: Learn about their prescribed treatment, and help them get used to it
items.3: Encourage them to keep going. Getting comfortable with a mask can take a few weeks, or even months
items.4: Reassure them that using CPAP doesn’t change how you feel about them
items.5: Support their efforts to be active, lose weight or quit smoking
items.6: Helping a parent? Before a hospital stay or sedation, make sure the care team knows they have sleep apnea, and pack their machine
items.7: Women more often have tiredness or trouble sleeping as signs, so listen to how they feel, not only to how they sound

8.note: Falling asleep at the wheel, or a near miss, can’t wait. See the warning signs at the top of Driving & Staying Safe.

9.title: First Nations and Inuit: NIHB coverage

items.1: The Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program covers CPAP and auto CPAP machines, masks and supplies for eligible First Nations and Inuit. Prior approval is needed
items.2: You can be eligible if you live in Canada and are a First Nations person registered under the Indian Act, an Inuk recognized by an Inuit land claim organization, or a child under 2 whose parent is eligible
items.3: Some people get these benefits through a First Nations or Inuit government, community or health authority instead, such as clients of the First Nations Health Authority in BC. Not sure? Contact your NIHB regional office
items.4: The request needs a diagnosis of sleep apnea with symptoms, your sleep study results and a prescription. It can start with a rental of up to 3 months, or with a request to buy. Buying needs test results that show your sleep improved on the machine
items.5: NIHB’s replacement guidelines allow up to: a machine every 5 years, and 2 masks with headgear, 2 tubes and 14 inlet filters a year. Each replacement needs a new prescription
items.6: Equipment comes from an enrolled respiratory provider with a registered respiratory therapist, or a registered nurse trained in managing respiratory conditions, on staff. The price covers mask fitting, set-up, follow-up and teaching
items.7: NIHB doesn’t cover the cost of the sleep test itself

9.note: Coverage is only for goods and services you get in Canada. Show your provider your client identification so they can confirm your coverage.
9.heldNote: Coverage for First Nations and Inuit is being reviewed with an Indigenous health partner and will appear here soon. Until then, contact your NIHB regional office.

10.title: Paying for it

items.1: You can claim a CPAP machine bought with a prescription as a medical expense on your income tax return
items.2: Many insurance plans cover CPAP equipment prescribed by a sleep doctor. Your insurer will ask for a copy of your prescription
items.3: Public coverage differs by province. For example, Alberta’s public health insurance doesn’t currently pay for CPAP equipment, while Ontario has a program that helps pay for a machine
items.4: In Ontario, the Assistive Devices Program pays 75% of its price for a PAP machine, or 100% if you get Ontario Works, the Ontario Disability Support Program or Assistance for Children with Severe Disabilities. It doesn’t pay for replacement masks or headgear
items.5: For Ontario’s program, you must buy from a business registered with it, and follow its steps before you buy. If you buy first, you pay the full cost
items.6: Veterans Affairs Canada’s respiratory equipment benefit includes CPAP, auto CPAP and bilevel machines, for eligible clients
items.7: The Canadian Lung Association has a grant program to help pay for children’s CPAP machines

10.note: First Nations or Inuit? See NIHB coverage above. Keep your receipts and your prescription. Insurers ask for a copy of your prescription, and receipts support a medical expense claim on your tax return.
